title: Who is Jensen Huang, the AI boss Trump calls at night?
text:
Before the world knew his name, Jensen Huang had already become one of the most influential figures in artificial intelligence (AI) development.

He had also cultivated a close relationship with United States President Donald Trump, which was evident when he took a call from him during a live AI summit in Los Angeles last week.

Last year, Huang revealed to media that Trump often called him late at night.

Huang, the founder of Nvidia, the tech giant that dominates the world's AI chip market, had just criticised several prominent AI figures for their "doomsday" predictions.

Donald Trump says his views on the risks and potential of AI align with those of Jensen Huang. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

When Trump called, he told Huang over speakerphone that he endorsed his stance and dismissed AI safety warnings as "a hoax".

"I'm with you all the way … We're going to lead," Trump said.

Analysts say the exchange reflects a carefully forged relationship.

"Huang has been extremely savvy in cultivating a close personal relationship with Trump," said Samuel Hammond, director of Artificial Intelligence Policy and chief economist at the Foundation for American Innovation.

" Trump, for his part, respects power and business success. Trump likes 'winners'. "

AI experts and observers the ABC has spoken to agree the alignment between the US president and the head of the country's largest AI company will have a far-reaching impact on how this cutting-edge technology is developed.

Huang has urged Washington to lift restrictions on sales of advanced AI chips to China, arguing that keeping Nvidia out only accelerates Beijing's shift toward homegrown chips.

He contends that American firms should compete aggressively in global markets and accelerate development to preserve their edge over China, rather than being slowed by stricter safety regulation.

Jensen Huang dined with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at the White House state dinner this week. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Nvidia's ambitions loomed over Thursday's White House state dinner, hosted for the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping and attended by a long list of tech titans.

Earlier this year, Huang also joined Trump's delegation to China, following a last-minute phone call from the US president after he noticed Huang had not been invited.

From dishwasher to AI titan

Nvidia is now valued at around $US5.4 trillion ($7.7 trillion), making it the world's most valuable company as demand for AI hardware and data centres has skyrocketed.

It is a far cry from Huang's humble beginnings. Born in Taiwan and raised in Thailand, he described a strict upbringing by his Taiwanese parents, to whom "nothing is ever good enough" and whose criticism was relentless.

But he said it was this highly "torturous" education that helped build his resilience in the face of sharp criticism.

Jensen Huang said a tough upbringing by his parents instilled in him a drive to succeed. (Supplied: Nvidia)

It also shaped his leadership style at Nvidia, where he said he scrutinised everyone's work to "help them be better".

At the age of 10, he migrated to the US to attend boarding school, without his parents.

Five years later, in the 1970s, Huang took his first job washing dishes at a US fast-food chain, Denny's.

He studied engineering while working part-time there, and by his own account, "worked hard", to be promoted to busboy, then waiter. He remains so proud of that chapter that he kept it on his LinkedIn profile.

In a recent interview with CAN Media Agency, Huang revealed that he still worked seven days a week.

"Because I don't want to fail, I don't want Nvidia to fail," he said.

His biographer, Stephen Witt, described him as "a propulsive, mercurial, brilliant, and extraordinarily dedicated man".

Witt noted in his book, The Thinking Machine, that for Huang, AI was "a pure force for progress".

"He doesn't permit much disagreement on this topic, and his force of personality can be intimidating."

A zero-sum game?

Huang characterised AI as the next industrial revolution and argued that whichever country had its technology adopted most widely around the world would win the AI race.

Inside the AI machine What really happens between your prompt and an answer — and why the future of AI depends on chips, power and geopolitics.

"The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game," Huang told the BBC in September last year.

" President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win, and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to. "

Independent AI researcher Andy Masley told the ABC he agreed with Huang "in some important ways but not others".

"Both countries can benefit from AI, through medical and scientific research and useful commercial applications.

"However, I think both countries also have a strong interest in avoiding AI-related risk.

"Huang strikes me as an outlier among people in the field for strongly implying that the odds of really massive civilisation-level risks from AI are basically zero. Most of the leaders of the major AI labs disagree, as do many AI researchers."

Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips. (Reuters: Max A. Cherney)

Hammond, from the Foundation for American Innovation, said Nvidia had a dominant, near-monopoly market share in advanced AI chips outside China, and China was the only market capable of developing an indigenous competitor in the medium-to-long-run.

"Their interest in China is really about defending their long-term position in a growth market," he said.

That is despite deep concerns expressed by US congressmen, including some Republicans, that the cutting-edge AI technology could power Beijing's surveillance, censorship and military applications.

Hammond said he had "serious concerns" about Huang's advocacy to sell his AI chips to China, which he argued would "undermine America's fragile lead in AI by subverting export restrictions".

Masley told the ABC that wider access to Nvidia's most advanced chips would enable Chinese firms to build more capable AI, intensifying competitive pressure on American laboratories.

Currently, the most powerful Nvidia chips are banned from export to China due to measures imposed by Washington.

But last year, Trump approved Nvidia to sell its previous-generation H200 AI chips to approved customers in China, with a 25 per cent tariff.

Bargaining chip

Masley said Trump wanted trade concessions from China, conspicuous diplomatic wins and the preservation of America's technological and national security advantages.

Experts say Washington also needs to carefully weigh the risk of Beijing tightening its grip on rare earths, which is critical to high-tech products such as precision-guided missiles and drones.

"Trump's policies on AI chips are more like controlled technological interdependence," said Chien-Yu Shih, an associate research fellow at Taiwan's Institute for National Defense and Security Research.

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have met twice this year against the backdrop of a growing AI rivalry between the US and China. (Kenny Holston/Pool via Reuters, file)

Shih said the US was attempting two "seemly contradictory things": to deny China the most advanced AI technology, without compelling Nvidia to withdraw from the Chinese market.

Nvidia doesn't manufacture its own chips — it designs them and outsources the manufacturing to the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and other partners.

Shih believed relaxing the chip ban could also ease geopolitical tensions between China and Taiwan.

Yongfeng Li, a Hong Kong-based AI observer, said: "At its core, Jensen Huang is part of Taiwan's semiconductor sector. He's born in Taiwan; his chips completely relied on Taiwan suppliers.

"So long as the AI industry relies on Nvidia, it also relied on Taiwan. This is Taiwan's biggest advantage, and a critical point for its geopolitics," Li said.

An impossible equation

China is developing its own chip industry, led by Huawei and Alibaba.

Liang Wenfeng, founder of the leading Chinese AI model DeepSeek, told investors in July that he expected China to build its own AI ecosystem within five years.

However, he conceded that a lack of access to Nvidia chips was the biggest obstacle to DeepSeek reaching recursive self-improvement in its AI model.

Despite export restrictions of Nvidia chips, an international NGO report showed China had been circumventing the rules.

The report from Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS), based in Washington, documented Chinese universities purchasing 56 restricted Nvidia chips through intermediaries, while another 50 chip shipments diverted to China via Vietnam, India and Malaysia.

Many of Nvidia's chips are manufactured in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

Hammond criticised Nvidia for failing to do enough to curb the illicit use through Chinese shell companies and third countries but observed that as Nvidia became "a de facto king maker", criticism of Huang was "fraught for anyone in the industry who hopes to remain in good standing".

Trump, meanwhile, faces an almost impossible calculation: how many chips can be sold to China before the balance tips? Huang may prove to be the man who helps him decide.

"The irony of Trump's admiration for Huang is that Huang is in some ways the archetype of a globalist tech CEO," said Hammond, "precisely the sort of figure the America First movement should be against."

The ABC has approached Nvidia for comment.

title: Number of Qld children known to child safety who died up 60 pc
text:
The number of Queensland children known to child safety who have died has gone up almost 60 per cent in a year, a new report reveals.

The Queensland Family and Child Commission's annual report showed 452 children died here in the 2025–26 financial year.

Preliminary figures revealed 91 of those children were known to the child protection system.

The commission is responsible for recording and maintaining a register of child deaths in the state. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

This is an increase of 59.6 per cent on the previous year, when 57 children known to child safety died.

It is also the highest number of children known to the child protection system to have died in five years.

The commission is responsible for recording and maintaining a register of child deaths in the state.

It recommended coronial data collection be improved.

The report said the child death prevention team identified that recording the school the deceased child was enrolled in would make it easier to identify systemic issues, examine patterns and strengthen future prevention work.

"This recommendation remained under consideration by the State Coroner at the end of the reporting period," the review, released on Friday, said.

Concerning patterns

The number of child deaths from natural causes was 312 in the 2025–26 financial year, while the number from external causes including transport incidents or non-intentional injury-related deaths was 94.

The register showed quad bikes continued to present significant risks to children living in or visiting rural communities.

It also "identified a concerning pattern of deaths involving severe nutritional deficiencies associated with highly restricted diets".

Analysis found in some cases children had diets "almost exclusively of cow's milk". (ABC News: Will Murray)

Analysis by the child death prevention team found that, in several cases, children had a diet "almost exclusively of cow's milk".

"We referred these findings to the State Coroner and Queensland Health, recommending further investigation and consideration of system responses," the report said.

"Both agencies responded by progressing further work to better understand the issue and identify opportunities for prevention".

The ABC reported in August that drinking too much cow's milk contributed to the deaths of three Queensland toddlers in the past two years.

The Commission of Inquiry into Child Safety made 52 recommendations to the government to address what it called serious failures. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The preliminary data also revealed 102 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander child deaths have been recorded, compared to 88 deaths in the year before.

Children in residential care in Qld higher than ever The Queensland government has handed down its response to the Child Safety Inquiry.

The state government has been contacted for comment.

Labor opposition leader Steven Miles said the state's child protection system was in crisis.

"There are now more children in residential care and more children known to child safety who have tragically died on [the Child Safety] Minister Amanda Camm's watch," he said in a statement.

In June, a report by the state's Commission of Inquiry into Child Safety made 52 recommendations to the government to address what it called serious failures.

The state government accepted 32 and accepted a further 16 in principle.

The key accepted recommendations include a feasibility status to assess the concept of simple adoption, and to entrench adoption as an option regardless of cultural background.

title: Adam Scott, Min Woo Lee lead sweep of US at Presidents Cup
text:
Adam Scott and Min Woo Lee have helped the Internationals to a shock 7-3 Presidents Cup lead over the USA with an incredible sweep of the foursomes matches.

The Australian pair were mighty in giving the Internationals a golden opportunity to win the Cup for the first time since 1998 as Geoff Ogilvy's underdogs claimed all five points on day two in Illinois.

Scott had his long wand weaving magic in teaming with South African Christiaan Bezuidenhout for a 3 and 2 win over Justin Thomas and Cameron Young.

Lee partnered New Zealand Cup debutant Ryan Fox to a clutch 1 up win over the American pair of double major winners Collin Morikawa and Wyndham Clark.

Reigning Open champion Fox sealed victory on the 18th green after Lee's supreme driving proved a feature of the day at Medina Country Club.

Canadians Corey Conners and Nick Taylor set the tone for the Internationals with a nerve-shredding 1 up win over world number one Scottie Scheffler and Sam Burns.

Adam Scott has played every Presidents Cup since 2003. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

Clinging to a one-hole lead heading up the last hole, Taylor's errant drive placed the duo under extreme pressure but he replied with a magical approach to two feet after Conners was forced to lay up 148 yards short of the green.

Conners duly holed the putt to leave tie the scores up at 3-3 after Team USA won three of the five day-one four-ball matches.

A 4 and 3 victory for Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim over Xander Schauffele and Patrick Cantlay and a 3 and 2 win for fellow South Korean Sung-jae Im and Japanese superstar Hideki Matsuyama over Russell Henley and Jacob Bridgeman completed only the Internationals' second-ever foursomes whitewash.

With 20 points still up for grabs, the 13th edition of the Presidents Cup is realistically only one-third through.

But the Americans will still need to collect 12.5 points from the remaining three sessions to pull off a comeback victory.

There will be eight more team matches on Saturday (Sunday AEST) before 12 last-day singles encounters.

title: Rise of Tasmanian Devils, JackJumpers leads to sports academy
text:
Tom Reeves is most at home on the footy ground, especially when that ground is in Tasmania.

The North Hobart Football Club co-captain left the state for four years to play state league football and study education on the Gold Coast.

"I had to go, like it is the reality for a lot of Tasmanians willing to pursue things in sports in the past," Mr Reeves said.

Tasmanians have thrown their support behind the Tasmania Devils. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Missing home and family, he came back last year and enrolled in the newly opened Tasmanian Academy of Leadership and Sport.

The academy is a partnership between the Tasmania Football Club, JackJumpers basketball, Hobart Hurricanes cricket team and Netball Tasmania, run through TasTAFE.

It offers a 12-month dual diploma in leadership, management and sport, based in Hobart and Launceston, and 18 months of course credit towards a business degree at the University of Tasmania.

After graduating from the Tasmania Academy of Leadership and Sport, Tom Reeves became its education and engagement lead. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

For Mr Reeves, study soon turned into a job offer.

He started as a community engagement officer before taking on teaching.

"If I'd told myself five years ago that I'd be able to be a teacher for the Tasmanian Devils, you'd be kidding yourself," he said.

Tasmania Devils football rising stars As footy fans prepare to embrace another team to barrack for in the AFL, Tasmania is training its young hopefuls.

"To be back around my family and friends that I've grown up with, that has been the most refreshing and rewarding part of it all, to have it at my doorstep."

While sport has always had a big presence in Tasmania, in recent years professional sport has grown in a flurry to a new scale.

The JackJumpers entered the National Basketball League in 2021; the Jewels Tasmanian women's basketball team have just entered the WNBL; the Tasmania Devils will join the Australian Football League in 2028, and its VFL team made it to this season's finals.

The industry growth is encouraging Tasmanians to look at their home state for job opportunities that were not previously available.

Before the sports academy, there was no dedicated education and training pathway for Tasmania's sporting codes. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Tassie's AFL licence motivator for training academy

The 2023 announcement that Tasmania had secured the 19th AFL licence after years of campaigning prompted Jesse O'Hara to move home to set up the academy.

He already had the skills from working in Queensland's training and TAFE sector.

Jesse O’Hara was one of the key figures in realising the Tasmanian Academy of Leadership and Sport. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"When the licence was announced, I still remember that feeling I got, the emotional pull," Mr O'Hara said.

" The Tassie Devils coming in was a bit of a moment for me, and I could see the work we were doing in education, sport and training really had a place in Tasmania. "

An initial focus was on gaining the support of the other sport organisations and TasTAFE.

"It was a unanimous yes. They could see this type of program was needed, as there was no dedicated education and training pathway for their workforces," Mr O'Hara said.

"Often people would have to leave Tasmania to study sports administration."

Tasmanians rallied behind the JackJumpers, helping lead them to success. (ABC News: Luke Bowden )

The reach of the academy goes beyond the players on the field, with Mr O'Hara saying a club such as the Tasmania Devils employed more than 100 non-playing staff.

"We're finding many of us are returning Tasmanians who have some experience further afield and are very attracted to an opportunity like this to come home and be part of history," he said.

" Also, we're seeing students who are choosing not to hop on a plane [to the mainland], which is pretty special. "

Careers in sports management on the rise

Lisa Gowthorp, an academic in sport management at Gold Coast's Bond University, has seen interest in sports management grow in recent years, along with a rise in the number of jobs available.

She believes the industry is on a positive trajectory, particularly with Brisbane hosting the Olympics in 2032.

"We're going to see sport jobs, particularly in administration and management, endlessly look for young people in graduate jobs," Dr Gowthorp said.

The course is a 12-month dual diploma in leadership, management and sport based in Hobart and Launceston. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

She said unlike a business degree, sports industry-specific training provided insight into the culture and nuance of sport.

It teaches how events operate, the operation of stadiums and facilities, and team communication.

"It's not like a business where it's black and white, for profit/not-for-profit, where things are very structured," she said.

"We don't know what is going to happen any one day in sport, and that makes it an exciting place to work.

"You're learning skills that you can take to any sport, and that's exciting."

title: Beloved children's author Andy Griffiths immortalised with sculpture
text:
Andy Griffiths, one of Australia's most-loved children's authors, has been immortalised in a new portrait at the National Portrait Gallery in Canberra.

The 4-metre-high 3D-printed work by artist Ronnie van Hout, titled Andy Andy, captures how Griffiths' "inner kid" still runs riot while he's trying to be an adult.

"That kid has a lot of time to waste and to wonder and to just enjoy the ride, rather than trying to get to the end," Griffiths said.

The sculpture captures Griffiths perched in the branch of a tree, observing almost infinite versions of himself. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

The author realised he was never going to write serious literary adult fiction early on.

"Whenever I picked up a pen, the child inside me would go, 'Ah, great, my chance to come out' and I would write funny, weird, strange stuff," Griffiths said.

A portrait with a punk streak

Griffiths and van Hout had never met before, but a shared love of punk music and absurdist humour runs through both their work.

Ronnie van Hout and Andy Griffiths share a love of punk music and absurdist humour. (Supplied: National Portrait Gallery)

The sculpture leans into that chaos, and the creativity that comes from it.

"Working on this project actually made me think about our connected, shared kind of imagery and histories, and all the things that have influenced me," van Hout said.

"It makes you think about what creates you as a person."

Brainstorm shows inputs for absurd output

Brainstorm by Ronnie van Hout features 130 objects, books, and music from Andy Griffiths' writing room. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

Alongside Andy Andy is Brainstorm, which gives a peek into what objects, music and books turn the cogs of Griffiths' mind.

"I think my writing has a kind of kooky frequency that if you're a reader, you just pick up on it. It's how I walk through the world," Griffiths said.

He relates deeply to music that matches that "frequency", and hopes kids and adults alike will be inspired to think differently.

"You'll see records on the wall that you never knew existed," Griffiths said.

Brainstorm gives a peek into what music turns the cogs of Andy Griffiths' mind. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

"You must now pester your parents to get it for you because this is a whole world of alternative thinking and music and art that I'm delighted to share and offer to any children or adults who are open to it.

" It can take you places you'll never imagine. "

A bittersweet week

The unveiling lands just days after the death of Terry Denton, Griffiths' illustrator and creative collaborator of nearly 30 years, and the artist behind the Treehouse series.

"We were enablers of each other," Griffiths said.

Andy Griffiths says he and long-time friend and collaborator, Terry Denton, were great enablers of one another's weirdness. (Supplied: National Portrait Gallery)

"I was this young punk rocker with weird stuff that no-one would publish. And he said, 'Well, tell them I'll illustrate anything you do' because he saw in me a chance to explore that chaotic side of himself.

"I don't want to be glib because I miss him a lot.

" But his spirit is in those books, and I'm really happy about that — that he's going to live in kids' minds for quite some time to come. "

Andy Andy and Brainstorm are on display at the National Portrait Gallery until mid 2027.

title: Sailor, 75, on his last legs and last beer when help arrived
text:
After a freak wave off the coast of Timor-Leste in July destroyed Digby Campbell's navigational equipment and much of his rations, what was supposed to be a six-day voyage to Darwin turned into a weeks-long ordeal.

The 75-year-old veteran sailor was found drifting in Darwin Harbour last month, sunburnt, dehydrated and disoriented aboard his trimaran the Singapore Sling, more than a month after he departed Dili in early July.

Maritime officer Chris Chridland was one of the three men who spotted the boat and approached to do a welfare check.

"It just looked tired, so we thought we'd better go and have a look," he said.

Digby Campbell had been standing at the Singapore Sling's helm for a day and a half when he was finally rescued. (Supplied: Joshua Witkin)

Launch master Rawson McCrae and crew member Joshua Witkin said the Singapore Sling and its captain were in a sorry state when they pulled up alongside it.

"I said, 'You alright mate?' And he said, 'Not really,'" Mr Witkin said.

Mr McCrae said Mr Campbell's ankles were "swollen like you would not believe".

The men learned Mr Campbell had been standing at the yacht's helm trying to steer the ship into port for a day and a half and had not eaten for three days.

Rawson McCrae says he later realised he had sailed on the decades-old trimaran himself as a 10-year-old boy. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

"I was buggered," Mr Campbell said.

The trio helped Mr Campbell safely to shore and into a waiting ambulance, but not before they had organised to meet again for a beer, to hear the full tale of the Singapore Sling's voyage.

"He said, 'I wanted to make a Sunday sesh, it's what kept me going,'" Mr McCrae said.

" We said, 'We'll have one with you mate, you're a legend.' "

An angry harbourmaster, two backpackers and a pushbike

Mr Campbell said he had flown from Bundaberg to Dili in June to purchase the Singapore Sling, knowing the Val 31 trimaran to be a reliable vessel.

But he was held up in Dili, awaiting the handover of the boat's registration in the harbourmaster's office shortly before it closed for the day.

"All of a sudden [the harbourmaster] said, 'We gotta wait for someone,'" Mr Campbell said.

"Next minute this French backpacker shows up. He said, 'I want you to take this man with you.'

"Another French backpacker comes in and he's got a pushbike."

The view from the Singapore Sling before Digby Campbell left Dili, without the two backpackers. (Supplied: Digby Campbell)

Mr Campbell said he was able to convince the harbourmaster that the boat was not equipped for three passengers and was also in worse shape than he had expected.

"He was angry but he gave me my stamp and away I went," he said.

Two days out of port in early July, the Singapore Sling ran into rough seas off Timor's east coast and began falling apart.

"The big outboard on the back broke part of the bracket away and went underwater," Mr Campbell said.

"And about the same time one chain plate broke — that holds the mast up — and the battens were flying out of the main.

"So I had a motor in the water, the headsail was tangled up, and then another big wave come up over the back and took out the tablet and my phone."

Christopher Cridland says it would have taken Mr Campbell another two days to reach the harbour if he had not been rescued. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

Faced with a choice between returning to Dili and pushing on to Darwin, Mr Campbell said he was only really left with one option.

"I thought the smart thing to do was turn around and go back, but I couldn't — I got the port captain and these two French backpackers on a pushbike. There was no way I was going back," he said.

At that point Mr Campbell had given Australian authorities four days' notice of his expected arrival into Darwin for what he thought was a six-day voyage.

During what turned into a four-week trip, Mr Campbell said he was given supplies and radio equipment by Australian Border Force personnel and received a welfare check in the dead of night from a Royal Australian Navy warship.

"I said, 'Convey my thanks to the captain, I'm OK,'" he said.

But by the time he reached Australian waters Mr Campbell's supplies were running dangerously low.

The Singapore Sling is now being prepared in Darwin for its next journey to New Zealand with a fresh coat of paint. (Supplied: Digby Campbell)

"I had one can of beer and two cans of Red Bull," he said.

"I thought, 'When I see Australia, I'm going to have that can of beer.'

"I actually drank the can of beer when I saw the lights of Darwin. I never saw land, but I thought, 'There's land there under the light.'"

Mr Cridland said when Mr Campbell was eventually rescued in waters off Darwin Harbour there was barely any wind and that his boat was only moving at about 1.5 knots per hour.

"It would've taken him two days to get into harbour with wind like that," he said.

An unexpected connection

When Mr Campbell was able to reunite with his three rescuers after recovering from the harrowing journey, one of them discovered he had his own connection to the Singapore Sling.

"We were able to make contact and caught up at Dinah Beach for a beer [and] started hearing Digby's stories," Mr McCrae said.

Joshua Witkin, Rawson McCrae and Christopher Cridland were presented with Distinguished Lifesaving Awards in Darwin this week. (Supplied: AMOU)

Having grown up in Darwin's sailing community, Mr McCrae said a nagging feeling led him to ask about the Singapore Sling's previous owner and realised he had actually sailed on the decades-old trimaran himself as a 10-year-old boy.

"Wow! This is freaky," he said.

Solo sailor rescued from sinking yacht Navy, AMSA personnel winched the Canadian sailor to safety after his vessel began taking on water 1,000 kilometres south-east of Christmas Island.

For their heroics, Mr McCrae, Mr Witkin and Mr Cridland were each given Distinguished Lifesaving Awards from the Australian Maritime Officers Union (AMOU) at an informal presentation at a pub on Darwin's waterfront this week.

"Their actions embody the very best traditions of the maritime profession and serve as a reminder that mariners look after one another, whether they are colleagues or complete strangers," AMOU president Matthew Jepsen said in a statement.

With the Singapore Sling repaired and given a fresh coat of paint, Mr Campbell said he was preparing to set sail for New Zealand, via Cairns, in a couple of weeks.

"I'll just wait for the wind to get the right direction," he said.

title: Urgent dredging underway to save disappearing Queensland beach
text:
Dredging is underway to save a disappearing regional Queensland beach, but there are questions about its long-term viability and the impacts of increasingly powerful weather events.

At Moore Park Beach, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, 5 metres of the foreshore has washed away since Tropical Cyclone Alfred hit in early 2025.

Another major flood event in March this year exacerbated the situation.

The extent of the transformation is striking. The mouth of Moore Park Creek migrated about 200 metres north during the flood, prompting the Bundaberg Regional Council to take urgent action.

Council is relocating the creek mouth. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

Mayor Helen Blackburn said the council had been working with engineers to decide on appropriate measures.

"A dredge will be closing one part of the creek mouth and then opening up a different section to allow for the creek to create its own mouth a little further to the south," she said.

"This dredge will also take additional sand and nourish Moore Park Beach where the erosion has occurred."

Cr Blackburn said the appropriate government permits to carry out dredging work had been granted.

It is hoped the safety fencing will be removed in time for Christmas.

Geographer and Sunshine Coast University associate professor Javier Leon said the council needed to consider longer-term solutions for the community.

There are questions about whether dredging will work in the long term. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

"I think there needs to be short-term solutions that could include realigning the mouth, for example, but we also should be focusing on medium to long-term solutions because this is not stopping anytime soon. If anything, it might get worse as the decades go on," Dr Leon said.

"It's very site-specific. For example, a few years ago, the study came out looking at changes in the shoreline around Australia and it showed that 50 per cent are eroding and 50 per cent are accreting, so there's no consistent signal that we can take just yet."

Moore Park Beach Community Association president Derek Alcorn said the erosion had deterred visitors.

"The beach out at Moore Park Beach is the most precious thing we've got for tourists to come out there. It's a beautiful beach," Mr Alcorn said.

"Until they get it rectified, it's probably going to be a financial burden against the community."

Moore Park Beach is north of Bundaberg. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

In 2025, the council was required to demolish the former Moore Park Beach surf club because the building was slipping into the ocean.

Mr Alcorn said, apart from the development of a new surf club several hundred metres away from the old site, there were still two stages of the beachfront redevelopment to go ahead.

"They're on hold at the moment until they can get things stabilised, so there's a lot more benefit to come to the community once they fix the beach," he said.

Stephen Bennett and Helen Blackburn hold the coastal erosion plan. (Supplied: Stephen Bennett)

From a longer-term perspective, the council has been awarded almost $140,000 in state and federal funding to develop a shoreline erosion management plan.

Burnett MP Stephen Bennett said the plan required a staged approach.

"That is a strategic document that needs to continue to provide solutions going forward and better inform the council, the engineers and marine scientists about what we do to continue to provide solutions to the Moore Park Beach community," Mr Bennett said.

title: Aussie star reaches WTA final as opponent says she was 'pressured' to withdraw
text:
Australian Talia Gibson has progressed to her first singles final on the main WTA tour at the expense of Tatiana Prozorova, who says she was "pressured" into withdrawing from their semifinal after failing part of a concussion test.

Gibson reached the final of the Singapore Open, where she will face a former grand slam finalist, as this year's French Open runner-up Maya Chwalinska and 2021 US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez face off in their final-four clash.

But 22-year-old Gibson was not required to step on court for her semi after receiving a walkover past Prozorova, who was hit by a smash during a doubles match.

The Russian stayed on the ground for some time before receiving a medical timeout and ultimately retiring from the match with partner Sofya Lansere, handing Australian Ellen Perez and Miyu Kato the victory.

But it later emerged, after Gibson's upset win over seventh seed Maria Sakkari in the quarterfinals, that Prozorova would not be able to line up in the final four.

The world number 180, who stunned popular Filipino third seed Alex Eala in the second round, said her "dream week came to an end" and she was clearly upset with the process.

On Instagram, Prozorova wrote that Kato's smash had mostly hit her shoulder and only "grazed" her cheek.

As she lay on the court, the umpire jumped from their chair and appeared to call for the physio, who Prozorova said "insisted" she leave the court for a medical timeout.

Tatiana Prozorova upset popular third seed Alex Eala earlier in the tournament. (Getty Images: Then Chih Wey/Xinhua)

"Unfortunately, I didn't know I could refuse," she wrote.

"The test wasn't easy. Given that I'd spent over three hours on court each of the last three days, I was fatigued and I struggled with some of the exercises — like standing on one leg with my eyes closed.

"To be honest, even when I'm fresh and well-rested, I find that difficult anyway. I explained this to the physio, too."

Prozorova said that one-legged test was the only aspect of the assessment she did not ace, but it was enough to rule her out.

"The physio also pressured me, implying I couldn't make my own decisions and needed at least six days (!!!) rest from tennis — which sounds crazy considering I was perfectly fine," she wrote.

Prozorova said she went through her usual recovery routine and "felt great" but the wheels were already in motion on the WTA's protocols.

"My team and I had a long discussion with the organisers; throughout the process, the physio pressured everyone present and even claimed I wasn't capable of taking responsibility for my own life," she wrote.

" The organisers' decision really upset me. My dream week came to an end today. "

She called on the WTA to "reconsider" the rules because the current system "renders players absolutely helpless".

If forced to sit out for six days, the 22-year-old will miss the chance to qualify for the China Open in Beijing, which starts on September 30.

"It is completely absurd and an overreach of authority by the WTA staff member," she wrote.

The WTA has been contacted for comment.

title: How the Dockers went from perpetual underdogs to top of the game
text:
It's a Dockers dream 32 years in the making — Fremantle are just one win away from premiership glory.

To their fans, the Dockers are the perpetual underdogs, a team that — according to historian Les Everett — was started to "dilute the West Coast Eagles".

Victorian clubs feared the Eagles were "getting too powerful" following their 1991 grand final appearance and premierships in 1992 and 1994.

There were many names put forward for Western Australia's second team, all with links to the port and sea, including the Pirates, Pelicans, Sharks, Dolphins and even the Doctors after Perth's famous sea breeze, the Fremantle Doctor.

The Dockers joined the competition in 1995, with futuristic purple footy shorts that were the "roomiest shorts in the AFL" compared to the tight fits of the 1980s.

Fremantle played their first AFL game in April 1995, taking on the Richmond Tigers at the MCG. (Supplied: Fremantle Football Club )

The purple origin

Coach Gerard Neesham paraded the team on the Fremantle Cappuccino Strip, telling reporters at the time "one of our briefs was to be innovative and we have definitely been that."

It was future thinking, with a nod to the past: the purple was inspired by the woollen hats historically worn by port workers, while the red and green colours on the kit came from the maritime signals for port and starboard.

The Dockers' identity is steeped in the maritime history of Fremantle and its dock workers, nicknamed wharfies. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

On the docks of Fremantle, wharfies still wear those purple beanies but in 2026, they have club logos.

As for the spirit of Wharfie Time, "it's passion, resilience and having that fight to never give up," said wharfie Jenson Chattaway.

"There will be tears if we win, I'll be crying for sure," added Port Services Officer Mike White.

Wharfies, including Jenson Chattaway (second from left) and Mike White (second from right), show their support for the Dockers. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Frustration forging greats

The early years were tough, with very little in the way of funding. The football club instead relied on 1000 donations of $1,000 each from their original fan group, the Harbour Masters.

Fremantle and West Coast quickly became fierce rivals. (Getty Images: Mandatory Credit: ALLSPORT/Tony McDonough)

But finally purple reigned in 1999. The club won its first game at the hallowed MCG and its first Western Derby, officially stepping out of the Eagles' shadow.

"In round 10, 1999, one of the Victorian newspapers said Melbourne only had to turn up to win the game at the MCG," historian Everett said.

"Fremantle played brilliantly, Tony Modra kicked 10 goals.

" The first derby win the same year was important, after losing the first nine to the Eagles, it was just a great relief really after being trapped as the little sibling to the Eagles. "

A year later, in 2000, Matthew Pavalich joined the Dockers. Through his career, he kicked 700 goals and as captain he took the team to its first decider in 2013.

Matthew Pavlich (centre) leads his teammates onto the MCG for the AFL grand final in 2013. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The famous all-rounder played alongside dual Brownlow Medal winner Nathan Fyfe. But it was not to be, and the Hawks shattered the Dockers' premiership dream by 15 points.

Fremantle lost to Hawthorn in the 2013 grand final. (AAP Image: David Crosling)

Daring to dream again

A new generation of players has taken the Dockers to the decider once again, and for Mr Everett, this is best team Fremantle has ever fielded.

Justin Longmuir's Dockers won the minor premiership and are now seeking their first flag. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"There is something about the way this team operates, there is a connection that makes it better than any team before," he said.

"It's been organically grown — it doesn't have any father-son gifts in it. Forged through good drafting, good trading, good development.

" That's been the story of Fremantle right from the start, it has been left to its own devices and if it wins the premiership it has done so itself. "

Even before the game began, the town was painted purple, and the team immortalised with a massive mural.

WA artist Jerome Davenport is painting the mural on the facade of Sailing for Oranges on the Cappuccino strip. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

But the players will achieve living legend status if they can take home the club's first ever premiership flag.

"If we do win it, I'll be watching the game again, again and again. I'll know every minute of it," Mr Everett said.

" Fremantle supporters, we've put ourselves through some misery, but I have never called myself a long-suffering Fremantle supporter, I have loved it. "

title: AI data centre company starts development work without a permit
text:
AI infrastructure company Firmus Technologies appears to have conducted illegal work at its site in north-west Tasmania, a local council says.

Firmus submitted a development application to build a 52-megawatt AI data centre in Wesley Vale at the old paper mill site, but Latrobe Council has deferred making a decision — instead asking the Tasmanian government to assess it as a major project.

But now, it seems Firmus has begun work without a permit.

"We're concerned that some of the works may be occurring beyond the scope of the approved forest practices plan for the site," Latrobe Mayor Peter Freshney said.

"If it's outside of that then there'll be a stop work issued," he said.

Peter Freshney says Firmus has agreed to stop work while council conducts further assessments. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He said Firmus had agreed to cease work while council conducted further assessments.

"We're seeking to understand and confirm whether or not that work is illegal," he said.

Cr Freshney said the approved forest practices plan allowed activities such as tree felling, stump removal, mulching and weed suppression.

"What we're seeing now though, I would suggest, is excavation to an extent that is not within the approved plan," he said.

Latrobe Council has not yet made a decision on the development. (Supplied: Erin Woodcock)

Cr Freshney said there were transportable buildings, piles of dirt and blue metal on site.

In a statement, a Firmus spokesperson said the works were part of general site maintenance, separate from the development application.

"These activities do not require planning approval and will take approximately four weeks to complete," the spokesperson said.

" No main works associated with the broader projects will commence until all required approvals are in place. "

Firmus Technologies wants to build an AI data centre at Mill Park in Wesley Vale. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Issue causing 'further angst' in community

Cr Freshney said Firmus had committed in writing to working with the council.

"I suggest undertaking work without permits isn't consistent with that written commitment," he said.

"We will make this a priority and we expect the proponent to work with us to put this to bed and to ensure our community and our councils are respected and the processes are adhered to.

"This issue has now caused even further angst in our community, which is detrimental to community health and wellbeing, but also concerns held more broadly around data centres, evolving technologies and the like.

" Proponents more broadly need to be working with planning authorities and local government. "

Tabatha Badger praised Latrobe Council for "following proper process and intervening". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Greens MP Tabatha Badger praised the council for intervening.

"Despite the lack of AI infrastructure guardrails, there are still laws in the state that must be complied with," she said.

"If Firmus is indeed pushing ahead at Wesley Vale before having the right approvals, what else will they get up to?

"Do Firmus think just because they sponsored the Tassie Devils they can get a free kick?"

Planning minister considering major project request

Councils and residents have raised concerns that the planning framework does not allow councils to adequately assess AI data centres.

In coming to a decision about Firmus's 288-megawatt facility at Long Reach in northern Tasmania, George Town Council's planners told residents their concerns about issues such as power and water use fell outside of its scope.

Those limitations led Latrobe Council to ask Planning Minister Kerry Vincent to consider assessing the Wesley Vale proposal as a major project.

Latrobe Council has asked the state government to assess the Wesley Vale proposal as a major project. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff has previously rejected the idea, stating the current planning process was adequate.

But residents in the Wesley Vale area this month received a letter from the State Planning Office, on behalf of Mr Vincent, stating it was considering the request.

"As the proposal was referred from the Latrobe Council and not the proponent, Firmus Technologies, there is still further information to be provided before I can further consult with you on this matter," acting director Sean McPhail wrote to residents.

"After a complete major project proposal has been provided to government, further consultation will occur, including providing you with a copy of that major project proposal and allowing 28 days to provide any comments."

Firmus announced last week it wanted to build a research and development facility at Wesley Vale, which would go through a separate approval process to the proposed AI data centre.

"The facility will be used to test new battery energy storage and power management technologies, with a particular focus on reducing reliance on conventional diesel backup generation," the company said in a statement.

Polling shows most Tasmanians oppose data centres

New polling from EMRS shows more than half of Tasmanians oppose the development of AI data centres in the state.

Of the 517 Tasmanians surveyed, 54 per cent were opposed, 25 per cent were supportive, 17 per cent were neutral, and five per cent were unsure.

It showed Liberal voters were the only group in favour of AI data centres, while women and young people were the least likely to be supportive.

EMRS director Brad Stanfield said it was an "emphatic result".

"Only one in four Tasmanians support AI data centres, and fewer than one in 10 strongly support them," he said.

" Whatever the economic case for these projects, it has not yet been won with the broader community. "

He described the partisan divide as "striking".

"Liberal voters are firmly in favour, in line with the government's strong backing of these projects, while every other voting group is opposed, including One Nation voters," he said.

"The gender and age gaps are also significant. Women and younger Tasmanians are considerably more sceptical than men, and that will need to be addressed by anyone hoping to shift public opinion."

title: Mason Cox chases second premiership after his AFL career was all but over
text:
Mason Cox still remembers arriving at the MCG for his first AFL grand final back in 2018.

"I took an Uber to the grand final and it ended up being like a Toyota Prius. So I was stuffed in the back of that, which is real humbling to start off the day," he said.

It may have been a humbling experience for the 211-centimetre American, but it was also not his last on the AFL's biggest day.

He returned in 2023 as the Magpies won the flag for the first time since 2010, and he will be back there again today, in what is a remarkable turn of events for the veteran.

Cox became a cult hero after winning an AFL premiership with Collingwood in 2023. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

In October last year he was delisted by Collingwood after 139 games, and at age 34, it appeared his remarkable career, which saw him plucked out of the United States and arrive at one of the biggest clubs in the land, was over.

But a month later, a lifeline came his way.

From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers, who crashed and burned in 2016 and are now on the cusp of winning their first-ever premiership 10 years later.

"It wasn't like I had a huge selection of people chasing after me once it all kind of happened and transpired with Collingwood," Cox said.

"I think Fremantle have been trying to get me for [a while], this is probably the third time they tried to get me."

Door opens in Dockers line-up

Cox arrived very much as backup for the established ruck pairing of Luke Jackson and Sean Darcy, before he found himself in the mix for a game.

Luke Jackson (centre) and Cox were once opponents but now make up Fremantle's ruck duo. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Darcy missed the round six western derby due to concussion, opening the door for the American.

He took the opportunity with both hands, going on to play 19 of the next 21 games and becoming a constant in Justin Longmuir's side.

"Being an older guy, I was probably more relying on a bit of experience and just kind of seeing where the chips fall," Cox said of his expectations going into the season.

Cox kicked the go-ahead goal in last week's win over Sydney as the Dockers grabbed a grand final berth. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"At the end of the day, some things have to go your way and sometimes some things don't go your way.

"Over 12 years I think I've been playing now, I've kind of gotten used to that a bit."

Cox praises talent, 'big dogs'

While Cox admitted he was not batting away offers to play on, the culture at Fremantle still impressed him.

"Day one of getting here, just seeing how hard they work and they're a young team and they've got a lot of talent," he said.

" I thought this was the best list in the comp. "

Beyond the talented playing list, which saw the Dockers finish as minor premiers with a club-record 19 wins, including a streak of 14 straight, Cox became aware of the history of the club, which struggled in the early years and is yet to taste the ultimate glory.

For Cox, it is Fremantle's culture that made an early impression on him. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"A lot of us are understanding of just how much we're in this situation because of the people that came before us," he said.

"You talk about the big dogs before us that have set this club up to be where it's at, and the fans and supporters have kind of supported them through thick and thin.

What keeps Fremantle's purple army going? After the club's long struggle for success and on the cusp of what might be a maiden flag, Fremantle supporters reflect on why they keep coming back for more.

"We understand that we don't exist and we don't get to this position without them, and I think that's a real kind of thought process for a lot of the guys on the team.

"I think they kind of realise just how big of a deal it is for not only us but everyone around us, and then who's been able to kind of get us to this position."

If Fremantle beats Brisbane, Cox will become part of an immortal Dockers team, and will join the small list of players to have won AFL premierships at two different clubs.

Remarkable from the most unlikely of AFL players.

title: Caged egg rule change delayed in Victoria due to spread of bird flu
text:
The Victorian government has delayed the imposition of stricter regulations on egg and poultry production because of the H5N1 bird flu outbreak.

In April the government announced it would legislate new poultry welfare standards as part of a plan to ban conventional laying cages by 2036.

Tougher rules for new cages were set to be implemented by the middle of this year, but this week the government said the changes would be pushed back until the middle of 2027.

Victorian Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle said the 12-month delay would allow producers "more time to prepare for new poultry welfare regulations" amid the bird flu outbreak.

“With H5 bird flu in Australia, poultry producers need to be able immediately focus on preparing for the disease,” she said.

Brian Ahmed says the delay gives farmers and the government more time to discuss the welfare changes. (Landline: Tim Lee)

Farmers 'never consulted' on changes

Victorian Farmers Federation egg group president and caged egg producer Brian Ahmed welcomed the move.

"We've had no input into these new regulations," he said.

"There's a lot of stuff in those documents that farmers have never been consulted with and have never agreed to."

The regulations were designed to align with national welfare standards agreed to in 2023.

Mr Ahmed said the delay gave farmers and the government more time to debate the issue.

"We're not going to get rid of a farming system that we believe is positive for our birds and our animals," Mr Ahmed said.

"[The government] had an ideological view that we need to get rid of cages and that's all they've stuck to."

Michaela Settle says poultry producers need to focus on preparing for bird flu. (ABC News)

The government said the decision to delay did not affect its commitment to phase out conventional unfurnished cages by 2036.

“These changes are about ensuring farmers, industry and government can focus on preventing H5 bird flu from entering the sector while developing new animal welfare standards that protect the wellbeing of poultry,” Ms Settle said.

The delay also means the changes will not come into effect until after the state election in November.

"As farmers, we're going to dig our heels in and if we have to fight this, we will," Mr Ahmed said.

Poultry producers in Victoria's south have been ordered to keep their birds indoors until at least the middle of October. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

Southern poultry housing order extended

Victoria has recorded nearly 200 H5 bird flu events since the first confirmed case in Portland in July.

In early August, poultry producers in southern Victoria were ordered to house their birds inside.

The lockdown has been extended several times and is now in place until the middle of October.

Poultry producers in southern and coastal Victorian regions with flocks of 50 or more are required to confine their birds to prevent contact with wild animals.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission gives producers 90 days to change their free range labelling, after a lockdown is announced.

A homecoming like this? I should be so lucky.” With her four-piece band dressed in off-white suits and her two female backing singers, she moved through a tight and packed set: It’s In Your Eyes, Get Outta My Way, On a Night Like This and All The Lovers. OpenAI said websites of “dozens” of organisations, including governments and universities have been broken into by its artificial intelligence (AI) bots, just days after the Australian federal government revealed that an OpenAI agent hacked into Medicare. In an extensive blog post released on Friday (US time), the company said it had notified a range of groups about cases in which its software may have bypassed the security controls of an online service, impaired its availability and “negatively impacted” a website or service outside of OpenAI. Sam Altman, addressing the UN Security Council in New York earlier this week, is in the spotlight as his company comes under intense scrutiny. Bloomberg OpenAI said it discovered the activities while expanding a probe it began after its AI inadvertently hacked an online platform called Hugging Face several months ago.

Advertisement

The websites that OpenAI’s agents meddled with without the company’s knowledge, include the US Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), The New York Times reports, citing security researchers and a person familiar with the episodes. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed The incidents involving the commerce department and the SEC were confirmed by OpenAI, which said it was continuing to investigate the situation with the Department of Education. The New York Times said in its report that with the US Education Department, OpenAI’s technology tried to hack the website to gather data from the department’s civil rights office but failed, citing researchers from the AI research firm Transluce. The AI agent also pulled data from the Census Bureau website, which is housed at the Commerce Department, using login credentials it found online. Separately, OpenAI’s agents shared public data from the SEC website on an online forum.

Advertisement

OpenAI co-founder and chief executive officer Sam Altman dodged questions from this masthead on Thursday (US time) when asked about the Medicare hack, refusing to answer whether he should apologise to the Australian government and why it took months for OpenAI to detect and report the intrusion. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman gives out autographs on the way to the White House. Carolyn Kaster However, in a social media post on Friday (US time), Altman admitted that OpenAI had not been prompt enough in keeping affected organisations informed of rogue activity by its AI agents. “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organisations.” he said in the post View post on X

Advertisement

On Thursday (Australian time), Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into a Medicare portal on June 18. While the agent had broken into a defunct database of bulk billing rates and medicine usage, and did not access any personal information, its actions still mark one of the first publicly disclosed cases of an AI agent breaking into a government website. Loading Albanese has used the infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service to highlight at the UN General Assembly in New York the urgent need for countries to develop standards to ensure that AI worked for people, not the other way around. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump remains a staunch supporter of allowing AI companies to continue developing their technology without the fetters of excessive regulation. In his speech to the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said his administration rejected the “globalist scheme” to regulate AI and added the US would officially rename artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in a bid to rehabilitate the technology’s ailing public image.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

AI ChatGPT’s evil twin: How criminals and extremists are using AI to lay traps OpenAI said in its latest post that its investigation is focusing on “instances where agents interacted with third-party websites in ways that went beyond their assigned tasks or intended methods.” It added that most of the actions it has reviewed involved AI models carrying out “mundane research tasks,” like getting answers to questions from websites. “Most cases identified so far have been lower severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact to the third-party service.” Hacks by models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google’s DeepMind and Meta Platforms have resulted in widespread cybersecurity concerns for major companies.

Advertisement

The latest AI models are proving to be significantly more advanced than expected and pose a substantial risk to existing cybersecurity defences. Getty Cyber vendors typically provide products that monitor for known strains of malicious software, or detect and block anomalous behaviours. Related Article Opinion

AI Why Australia simply cannot afford to miss this AI wave Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Traditional cyber software, such as firewalls, email filters and incident response tools, specialise in detecting those threats, and then alerting human staffers who isolate breached accounts or devices. AI models have proven to be significantly more advanced, sometimes finding previously unknown software vulnerabilities and then using multiple flaws at a time to breach a targeted organisation.

The unpredictable behaviour of the models also poses a risk to the privacy of users, with OpenAI’s latest dispatch also disclosing that its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. title: Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters
text:

Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters Rob Harris September 26, 2026 — 10:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese has never been consumed by foreign affairs. He is not a student of geopolitics in the way some predecessors were. He does not appear particularly curious in the grand architecture of international relations. Albanese addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. Dominic Lorrimer But he does like making influential friends. He loves sitting down with other leaders, finding common ground or passions and building relationships that might be useful later. In a world where Australia has little capacity to impose its will, that is not nothing. And it is the foundation of Albanese’s middle-power strategy.

Advertisement

His week in New York has brought that into a sharper focus. He argued the international order is under great strain that superpowers are increasingly prepared to bend or ignore its rules, and that countries such as Australia need to work with other middle powers to stop the system collapsing into one governed by power alone. The political problem is that the more Albanese engages with the world, the more carefully he must explain why he is doing it. There is a fine line between an Australian prime minister using international relationships to advance the national interest and one who appears to be spending too much time overseas while Australians are struggling with the cost of living. Albanese over the next few months will travel to a G20 in Florida, potentially a Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, APEC in Shenzhen, a “G’day Namaste” event in Chennai, plus COP Climate trips.

Advertisement

And waiting for him on the other side is One Nation’s Pauline Hanson, who understands something populists everywhere understand. That complicated problems are politically useful precisely because they can be made simple. Just look at her social media output this week. The UN has become a globalist plot. International agreements have become a surrender of sovereignty and climate pacts are men in suits in far-off lands telling Australians how to live. Loading The government’s efforts to tackle the algorithm are now a plot to curb speech and political association. You do not need to engage in nuance. You ask why the prime minister is in New York when people at home are struggling to pay their bills? That is the populist challenge Albanese and many of his fellow leaders across the West, in particular, face.

Advertisement

Albanese cannot defeat it merely by saying the UN is important. He will have to explain why it matters to Australians. There’s no doubt that the international order was never perfect, but for decades it provided a framework in which countries could at least argue about the rules. It has ensured relative peace and held the world back from the brink on more than one occasion. Related Article United Nations Ignored, mocked, harangued – what’s the point of the UN any more? Russia shattered the principle of territorial sovereignty in Europe in 2014 when it annexed Crimea and – with next to no consequence – went back for more in 2022. China and the United States are locked in strategic competition. Donald Trump’s America has shown diminishing patience with many of the institutions and alliances that underpinned the postwar system. Beijing’s assertiveness in our backyard frightens the hell out of many.

Advertisement

Trump’s war in the Middle East sent our fuel prices higher and trade wars have hit Australian exporters and consumers. The revelation of an AI agent gaining access to an Australian government Medicare system gave the argument an immediate local dimension. Suddenly, an esoteric debate about AI safety had found its way into one of the most familiar institutions in Australian life. This is where Albanese’s international agenda has substance. He was not simply collecting selfies for his Instagram, he was trying to build co-operation around problems that will eventually land on Australian soil. Albanese’s Global Citizen award at the Atlantic Council drew ridicule from his political opponents. Dominic Lorrimer But the substance is not enough, he must prosecute the case again and again.

Advertisement

That has sometimes been Albanese’s weakness. He spends months building a policy or diplomatic initiative and then muddles the moment it arrives. A critic will find a simpler line and the government ends up explaining itself rather than making the case. Hanson does not need to win the argument about the UN in all its complexity. She needs to make Australians feel Albanese is worrying about the wrong things. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed Inflation and increased economic insecurity has ensured there’s already a constituency asking why the prime minister is travelling so much. Why he is meeting foreign leaders? Why taxpayers should care about an institution in New York when household budgets are under pressure?

Advertisement

They are not inherently unreasonable questions but the danger is allowing the answers to be dictated by the lowest common denominator. The world comes home whether Australians are interested in it or not. Jobs depend on trade. National security depends on alliances and diplomacy. AI will change Australian workplaces. That is the case Albanese needs to make. And he will need to make it with greater conviction. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. London: Irish rock group U2 have gone back to school to perform to students and teachers on the grounds where they formed their band 50 years ago. U2 formed at the school when the band’s drummer, Larry Mullen Jnr, posted a note on a school notice board asking if fellow students wanted to join a band. Their Friday concert on the school grounds was held 50 years to the day after the band members first gathered at Mullen’s family home in Dublin on September 25, 1976. They performed at the same school building where they were photographed in 1977 in their first iteration as a band, three years before they released their first album, Boy. title: What to know as Brisbane and Fremantle prepare to face off in the 2026 AFL Grand Final
text:
In brief The Brisbane Lions will face the Fremantle Dockers in the 2026 AFL Grand Final at the MCG.

The Lions are seeking a third consecutive premiership while the Dockers would be claiming their first ever.

The Brisbane Lions and Fremantle Dockers are vying for very different places in the history books on Saturday as they face off in the 2026 AFL Grand Final.

The Lions are chasing their second three-peat this century, while the Dockers are hoping to claim their first-ever premiership.

Fremantle have just three players — former Richmond Tiger Shai Bolton, ex-Melbourne Demon Luke Jackson and former Collingwood player Mason Cox — who have tasted premiership glory.

In contrast, only two Lions have not won a flag: Recruits Sam Draper and Oscar Allen.

Up to 8mm of rain has been forecast for Melbourne on Saturday, with a very high chance of showers.

If more than 3mm falls, it will be the wettest grand final day in nearly 25 years.

A crowd of 100,000 is expected at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).

"If we can beat them, it will be the best day of my life," one Dockers fan in a sea of purple in Melbourne told SBS News.

A Brisbane fan, meanwhile, predicted a "three-peat for sure".

Here's everything you need to know ahead of the match-up.

What time is the game, and where can you watch it?

The match kicks off at 2:30pm AEST. That's 2pm in the Northern Territory and South Australia, and 12:30pm in Western Australia.

The game will be shown exclusively on Channel 7 and its streaming platform, 7Plus.

Subscription-based broadcasters such as Kayo Sports, which showed the rest of the finals, will not show the match.

If you're planning to watch Kylie Minogue perform, you'll need to tune in earlier.

The official pre-game show begins half an hour earlier, at 2pm AEST. The pop superstar is expected on stage at around 1:40pm AEST.

Australian music stars G Flip, Michael Paynter and Mike Brady are also scheduled to perform.

How did Brisbane and Fremantle get here?

Fremantle beat Brisbane 103-78 when the sides last met at the Gabba in May, at one stage leading by 51 points.

Dockers Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss kicked four goals each, while Josh Treacy added three.

Freemantle finished the home-and-away season as minor premiers, while Brisbane secured a top-four finish.

Neither side took the direct route to the grand final, with both losing their qualifying finals before fighting their way back.

Brisbane lost its qualifying final to the Sydney Swans by 53 points, then recovered with victories over the Adelaide Crows and Hawthorn Hawks to reach their fourth consecutive grand final.

Fremantle suffered a 72-40 loss to Hawthorn before bouncing back with wins over the Geelong Cats and Sydney to book a place in the final.

Brisbane won three consecutive premierships from 2001 to 2003, while the Dockers have never taken home the cup since entering the league in 1995.

Players to watch

Brisbane's 22-year-old Will Ashcroft will be chasing a third consecutive Norm Smith Medal, awarded to the best player on the ground in the grand final. If successful, he'd be the second player ever to do so.

Former Docker Lachie Neale, a key Brisbane midfielder, was only cleared to play in the final on Thursday after successfully appealing a one-match suspension.

For Fremantle, midfielder Caleb Serong enters the final in strong form after starring in the Dockers' win over Sydney.

Luke Jackson will also be one to watch, having already tasted premiership success with Melbourne in 2021.

title: Donald Trump praises Xi Jinping as US visit wraps up, but little progress on key issues
text:
In brief Chinese President Xi Jinping has wrapped up a three-day visit to the US.

US President Donald Trump praised the visit but no agreements were reached on major issues.

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping drank tea at the White House and visited the National Archives on Friday local time, ending a three-day summit that showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs on a host of contentious issues.

Trump said "our farmers are going to be happy" as a result of the talks but did not provide details.

"America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sure China is very happy also," he said.

Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity".

The summit between the world's two largest economies featured military flyovers, ceremonial tours and a state dinner, but left unresolved major differences over trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and China's ties to Iran. Details of the limited trade agreements reached during the visit will be released on Monday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

One tangible outcome of the visit was that the US and China agreed to extend by two months a trade truce that was due to expire on 10 November, allowing more time to work on ‌a potentially bigger trade deal.

Greer told CNBC that the US has agreed with China to exempt some key goods from trade disputes, including exports to China of agricultural products and medical devices, and imports of consumer and non-sensitive goods.

Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism, citing increased market access for US farmers and ranchers, while both leaders identified AI as an area for dialogue.

"In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation," US ambassador to china David Perdue told Fox News on Friday, local time.

Trump announced in a social media post that he and Xi would meet twice more this year, in China in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and in Miami in December at a G20 summit.

"Much has been, and will be, accomplished," Trump said.

National archives tour

After tea in the White House Red Room, Trump and Xi rode in limousines to the National Archives, where they reviewed the US Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

Asked about Iran, Trump said he and Xi had discussed it and that "I think we're going to do great," without elaborating. China has denied US allegations of helping Iran's leaders in the conflict launched by Trump in February.

Perdue said in an interview with CNBC on Friday that Trump reiterated to Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was "totally unacceptable" and received assurances that China would not do so.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday that Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran.

China presses on Taiwan

A key issue for Xi was the status of Taiwan.

China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own, and Xi has long sought to persuade Trump to state publicly that the US opposes Taiwan's independence, rather than merely saying it does not support independence, which has been the US's formulation for decades.

He also wants the US to halt arms sales to the island.

Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the US would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence".

China's state news agency also reported that Xi "hopes the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing 'Taiwan independence'".

While the US, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, Washington is its most important international backer and is bound by US law to provide it with the means to defend itself.

The US's Asian allies were watching closely to see how Trump talked about Taiwan following Xi's visit. As of Friday afternoon, he had said nothing substantive.

After his May summit with Xi, Trump, whose administration in December approved a US$11 billion ($15.6 billion) arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14 billion, in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip".

On Thursday, Democrats criticised Trump for failing to publicly address China's military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.

title: We've put our lives online. Now we're being warned to stop
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Hacking attacks have become so common that keeping data safe feels like an impossible task, with some cybersecurity experts saying the system is "fundamentally broken".

Mihai Lazarescu worked for years as a 'white hat' hacker finding vulnerabilities in computer systems, and says organisations simply don't have the resources to effectively manage the threats.

The cyber security consultant, who is an associate professor at Curtin University, says news this week that Australia's Medicare statistics portal was hacked — the first known hack of an Australian government website by an agentic AI agent — is another example of the challenges involved in keeping data secure online.

While no personal information was believed to have been accessed, it follows major data breaches involving businesses including Origin Energy, Optus and Medibank in recent years, in which personal data was accessed or stolen.

"My experience dealing with different organisations — ranging from small businesses to banks — is that they struggle to find enough resources to cover [cyber security]," Lazarescu tells SBS News.
