Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Even if they have the funds to protect their systems, finding people with the right skills is difficult.

The reality is that if people want to get to your data [and] it is available, they'll probably find a way to do it.

Lazarescu says continuing to place data online at the same rate "makes no sense" and the system is "fundamentally broken".

"We can't protect things, and now you have this emergence of automatic agents, why do we keep going it?"

Lazarescu says consumers need to push for change.

"If there's no pushback, this is going to keep going."

Should we go back to paper records?

In recent years, there's been a trend towards putting everything online, but given the security risks, Lazarescu questions why it's necessary for businesses, especially telcos and power companies providing essential services, to store their customer data on the internet.

These businesses have millions of customers, which means a cybersecurity breach has the potential to impact significant numbers of people.

Almost 10 million people had personal information accessed in 2022 when Optus' system was hacked, and around 10,000 had their data published on the dark web.

Customer data of mobile phone service provide Optus was compromised after a cyber attack in 2022. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

The hack of Origin Energy in July impacted almost one million current and former customers.

The number of hacking attacks is rising, with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner saying it received 1,205 data breach notifications in 2025, an increase of 8 per cent from the previous year.

Until a system is developed that enables information to be stored securely, Lazarescu says some businesses should consider returning to paper records, something that was functional in the past.

I've seen all kind of benefits being touted [to putting stuff online]. I haven’t seen yet any evidence that [it's] paying off.

Lazarescu points out the internet is essentially "unsecurable", arguing its underlying protocols were designed in an era when computers were primarily being used to link academics at different universities and assumed users were trustworthy.

"At the fundamental level [it] can't be secured unless we have an internet 2.0, and I can’t see anybody trying to do that," he says.

This makes putting stuff online a "comprehensively bad thing to do".

But Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer at the School of Computer Sciences and Engineering at the University of New South Wales, is sceptical about whether returning to paper records is practical.

She says technology has advanced and a significant increase in printing could also increase carbon emissions.

"The only solution I can see is public awareness and sharing less data, and companies collecting less data," Masood tells SBS News.

Rethinking data collection

While companies should be minimising the amount of personal information they hold, they often have limited incentives to delete data once it has been collected. Masood says many companies earn money from selling data.

It’s now common for businesses to ask for personal details from customers even when some of that information may not be essential to providing the service.

Masood points to Medicare card details being stolen during the recent Quest Apartment Hotels data breach.

Why do you need the Medicare [details to rent an] apartment?

The Quest hack raises questions about not only what information businesses collect, but also how long they retain it. Some impacted customers told the media they had last interacted with the business years ago.

Masood says data should only be stored when it is needed, and then deleted after a certain time period, including when a person dies.

While fines of up to $2.5 million for a person, and up to $50 million or other substantial penalties for a company, depending on the circumstances, can be issued for privacy breaches in Australia, Masood points out that laws are often not enforced.

She believes companies operating in Australia should be audited to ensure they are meeting the requirements of the Privacy Act 1988. This regulates how government agencies as well as some organisations, including those with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, handle personal information.

Changes should also be made so that people are given user-friendly and concise information about companies' privacy policies, instead of pages of terms and conditions they don't understand.

Masood says customers need simple information about what type of data is stored on business servers, how it is used, why it is needed, the potential consequences of this data storage, as well as who they can contact with issues.

"It's not a difficult task, it's just that companies don't want to do it."

More accountability needed

Jacqueline Boaks, a lecturer at Curtin University who specialises in business ethics, says there's often a sense of inevitability around AI and a sense of powerlessness that anything can be done to stop it, but she argues that societies have well-established laws to hold people morally and legally responsible for creating and releasing a product that does harm.

"We shouldn't forget that, just because something's digital and not physical," she tells SBS News.

We as a community and as the government need to have an expectation morally and ethically around who is accountable and who is responsible when [hacks] happen.

Boaks says it's impossible for individuals to oversee how their data is managed by companies or to opt out of services such as Medicare.

"[This] is a pretty vulnerable place to be, but it does seem to be exactly the kind of thing that we have a right to expect governments to protect us from," she says.

"That's one of their core roles."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese indicated support for regulating artificial intelligence at an international level during a speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week. Source: AAP / Sarah Yenesel/EPA

But Boaks says there's often a disconnect between the level of harm done through these data leaks and the consequences faced by companies.

Lazarescu agrees the consequences are not serious enough for companies to change their practices.

What happens when you have a breach? Do you see anything in terms of people being held accountable? Organisations being held accountable?

Lazarescu, who grew up in Romania under Communist Party rule, is also sensitive to what could happen if more aspects of people's lives move into digital systems, particularly if governments can easily erase people.

"To me the biggest problem with putting stuff online is that you can also modify it online."

What can people do to protect their data?

Leaders such as United States President Donald Trump have rejected the need for stronger AI regulation, and Trump has also criticised Australia's plan for digital duty of care laws that would give residents the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds.

But Lazarescu says this doesn't mean every American agrees with the Trump administration's position.

People have a lot more power and they need to be engaged and tell the politicians enough is enough.

At an individual level, Lazarescu and Masood warn against sharing anything online unless it is absolutely necessary.

This includes posting on social media, which can allow companies to build detailed profiles of users, avoiding unnecessary sharing of documents such as passport copies, and not entering sensitive details into AI programs such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and other large language models.

"It's very crucial now," Masood says. "You need to be minimising the data yourself."

title: Extra cash for some Australians — and a card surcharge shake-up looms
text:
Major Australian companies are sending billions of dollars to shareholders’ bank accounts as dividend payment season ramps up.

BHP, which is Australia’s largest listed organisation, delivered US$5 billion ($7.12 billion) in dividends to its investors on Wednesday.

That means its 450,000 retail shareholders may have received a fully franked final dividend of $1.38 for each share they hold in BHP.

It’s been a big year for the so-called “Big Australian” after copper became the company’s largest earnings contributor for the first time.

The nation’s most widely held stock is Telstra, though, with an estimated 1 million shareholders.

On Thursday it delivered its final dividend of 10.5 cents per share, paying out $1.2 billion dollars over the last financial year.

Of course, not all shareholders elect to receive dividends into their bank account, with some opting to reinvest that payment instead.

Millions of Australians have exposure to shares like BHP and Telstra through their superannuation fund.

Credit and debit card surcharges are going

It might be worth paying closer attention at the checkout next week to see how businesses are handling new credit and debit card surcharge rules.

From 1 October, those surcharges will be banned, eliminating the fee that is added to the price of goods and services.

It means the advertised price of a product should be the price you pay at the checkout.

Right now, a $5 coffee, for example, might actually be $5.08 when a surcharge is applied.

While the RBA has reduced some background fees associated with card payments to help small businesses make the change, they’ll still incur an expense, which means many will be forced to decide whether to absorb it or pass it on to customers.

So, from 1 October, will that $5 coffee still be advertised as $5, or will it go up to $5.08 or more?

Sarah Megginson from consumer group Finder says some small businesses may look to other forms of payment to reduce costs.

“You can use PayID and bank transfers, which transfer instantly, so you might see small businesses turn to these more affordable ways to accept cash,” she told the SBS On the Money Podcast.

Some larger businesses are doing away with card payments altogether as a direct result of the changes.

DEFT, an online secure payment system used by thousands of renters and homeowners, no longer accepts debit or credit card payments, instead pointing customers to payment options like PayID, BPAY or Australia Post.

To fund the changes, banks are also making adjustments through rewards cards, annual fees and bonus points restructuring,

Not all fees and surcharges are disappearing with these new rules, though, because they don’t extend to weekend or public holiday surcharges, booking fees, or service fees.

Interest rates may still rise despite a higher jobless rate

Earlier this week, Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock warned the unemployment rate may need to rise to as much as 5 per cent to help ease inflation, which in turn could lower interest rates.

Fresh ABS data on Thursday revealed more people are now in the workforce or looking for work, which could be a sign of cost of living pressures, while of the near 40,000 jobs created last month, they were all part-time, suggesting many may have been related to Census workers.

The headline jobless rate has climbed from 4.5 per cent to 4.6 per cent, which is a near five-year high.

Westpac senior economist Pat Bustamante says the RBA is still likely to lift interest rates on Tuesday.

“We think a September hike is locked in and reflects the data we’ve already seen,” Bustamante said. “Going forward, particularly in November, if the labour market eases a bit more than what they’re expecting, we can see them pause and wait.”

Higher inflation will likely prompt the bank to pull the trigger, which is only likely to get worse, according to HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham, who has two more interest rate rises this year pencilled in.

Bloxham says this is because overseas factors are adding to inflation, like higher fuel prices from the Middle East war, unfavourable weather and El Niño driving up food prices, and the AI investment boom.

title: Last-minute Rayan equaliser denies Socceroos famous win against Brazil
text:
A last-minute header from Brazilian substitute Rayan salvaged a 1-1 draw with Australia in a thrilling international friendly in Townsville on Friday.

Rayan headed the ball home in the 95th minute to deny the hosts what would have been only their second win over the South American giants.

It was a fitting result from two evenly-matched teams who gave everything in front of a sell-out crowd in the North Queensland city.

A superb free kick from Nestory Irankunda had looked enough to give the Socceroos an upset win.

title: Why Victoria may be millions of dollars better off with this AFL Grand Final match-up
text:
IN BRIEF Grand Final weekend could generate up to $75 million in economic activity for Victoria, according to one estimate.

But a sport business expert says the actual net benefit could be closer to $20 million to $25 million.

An all-interstate AFL Grand Final is expected to deliver a bigger economic boost to Victoria than a match between two Victorian teams.

Fremantle and Brisbane will meet at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in front an expected crowd of 100,000 people on Saturday in just the second all-interstate Grand Final since Victoria introduced its Grand Final Eve public holiday in 2015.

And tens of thousands of supporters travelling from Western Australia and Queensland are expected to pour money into Melbourne's hotels, restaurants, bars and other businesses.

RMIT University Professor Angel Zhong estimates Grand Final weekend could generate up to $75 million in economic activity for Victoria.

She says an all-Victorian derby could generate roughly a third of that figure because much of the money spent by local supporters would simply be redirected from elsewhere within the Victorian economy.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But Professor Hans Westerbeek, a sport business expert at Victoria University, says while the underlying argument is sound, the headline figure does not necessarily represent the amount Victoria ultimately gains.

"The Grand Final brings genuinely new money," he told SBS News.

But after accounting for money that leaves the state or economic activity displaced by the event, he estimates the real net benefit could be considerably lower.

So, where does the $75 million come from?

Zhong said the difference between an interstate and an all-Victorian Grand Final largely comes down to where supporters’ money originates.

"When interstate fans fly in, stay in hotels and eat in our restaurants, that is genuinely new money entering Victoria," she said in a statement.

"When people go to a local derby, they are mostly redirecting spending they would have made in the state anyway."

Westerbek agreed. Using what he described as a "back-of-the-envelope" calculation, Westerbeek compared a Grand Final in which about 90 per cent of spectators were Melbourne-based with one in which half the crowd travelled from interstate.

In the first scenario, he estimated roughly $5 million in value could be added to the Victorian economy.

READ MORE Suspended Swans players to make first public appearance since hotel scandal

If about half the crowd was interstate, he said that could rise to around $20 million to $25 million.

But, he said the gross visitor spend could be considerably higher.

Westerbeek estimated interstate visitors staying for two nights and spending on accommodation, food, drinks and tourism could generate around $60 million in visitor expenditure alone.

But emphasised that is not the same thing as Victoria being $60 million better off.

The money that doesn't make the headline figure

Westerbeek said headline economic impact figures can also be reduced by what economists call "displacement".

For example, some visitors who might otherwise have travelled to Melbourne could avoid Grand Final weekend because accommodation is booked out or more expensive, he said.

Their spending would therefore be replaced by that of visiting AFL fans, rather than representing entirely new economic activity.

That is separate from the substitution effect identified in RMIT's analysis, where spending by Victorian fans may simply be redirected from elsewhere in the state.

"There is definitely an influx of money, but there's also an outflow that is often not calculated in those headline figures," Westerbeek said.

READ MORE The numbers raising new questions about Australia's future wealth

Even money spent getting to Melbourne does not necessarily remain in Victoria.

Westerbeek said airfares, for example, largely go to airlines and travel operators that may be headquartered elsewhere.

What about Victoria's Grand Final public holiday?

For hospitality businesses packed with travelling football supporters, the public holiday the day before Saturday's big game can provide another day of strong trading.

But other businesses may face higher wage bills through public holiday penalty rates, fewer customers or an entire day without normal operations.

Zhong said whether the public holiday benefits a business depends heavily on its industry and location.

A restaurant near the MCG may have one of its strongest trading days of the year despite higher wage costs, while a business dependent on office workers could face higher costs and lower demand.

But a café reliant on office workers or a suburban restaurant with little connection to the game could face higher wage costs and fewer customers, or decide not to open at all.

Westerbeek said the wider loss of a normal working day was another factor that headline economic-impact estimates do not always capture.

For workers rostered on, penalty rates provide additional income.

But from a whole-of-economy perspective, Westerbeek said the lost productivity among sectors that shut down should also form part of any assessment of the weekend's financial impact.

"It certainly isn't something that is being featured or calculated when we talk about ... the headline reported benefits," he said.

That does not mean he believes Victoria loses from hosting the Grand Final.

"It is [a success]," he said.

"But it's not as substantial as the $75 million in terms of the headline number."

Melbourne's payoff goes beyond one weekend

Westerbeek told SBS News that the economic impact of the Grand Final is not limited to what visitors spend over the weekend, with Melbourne also deriving longer-term value from its reputation as a major events city.

Melbourne has spent decades positioning itself as a major-events city, with the AFL Grand Final sitting alongside events including the Australian Open and Formula One Australian Grand Prix.

Westerbeek said individual sporting events should therefore not necessarily be assessed in isolation.

"The AFL Grand Final is not a once-a-year kind of thing. It is part of a portfolio of events, a year-round calendar," he said.

Rather than suddenly transforming Melbourne's tourism economy each September, he said the Grand Final helps sustain the infrastructure, hospitality industry, expertise and reputation the city has built around major events.

"The Grand Final maintains Melbourne's reputation rather than building it," he said.

Evidence that a single event can create sustained tourism growth is relatively weak, Westerbeek said.

Melbourne's advantage is that the next major event is never particularly far away.

"It's not a peak moment," he said.

"It is a pulsating moment. It's one of many events that keep Melbourne, justifiably, as Australia's, maybe even one of the world's, major event and sports capitals."

The Australian Open tennis tournament is another big annual sporting event that draws visitors to Melbourne. Source: Getty / karenfoleyphotography

And while an interstate Grand Final may inject more outside money into Victoria, Westerbeek said the comparison misses something else entirely.

An all-Victorian Grand Final can generate social benefits for locals, including a sense of identity, pride and connection — that are difficult to attach a dollar figure to.

Those benefits may never appear in an economic-impact calculation.

But, he said, they are still part of what the Grand Final is worth.

title: Israeli footballer Saied Abu Farchi sent off after gun gesture goal celebration
text:
In brief Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi was sent off after using a corner flag to mimic a gun in a goal celebration.

Austria won 3-1, while Cody Gakpo denied Jürgen Klopp a winning Germany debut with a late equaliser.

Israel forward Saied Abu Farchi was sent off for celebrating his goal against Austria in their 3-1 UEFA Nations League defeat on Friday by using the corner flag to simulate a gun.

Abu Farchi headed home in the 55th minute to bring Israel level after Austria had taken the lead through a Romano Schmid penalty before halftime in the game in Linz.

The 20-year-old ran to the corner flag, grabbed it and made a gun-firing gesture during his celebration.

The referee had booked Abu Farchi four minutes earlier for a foul and showed him a second yellow card for the celebration, followed by a red, leaving Israel with 10 players.

Austria regained the lead in the 90th minute through Phillipp Mwene, who netted following a cross from Paul Wanner. Sasa Kalajdzic added a third in stoppage time with a close-range finish.

title: 'Not a coincidence': Opposition questions timing of Albanese's OpenAI hack reveal
text:
In Brief James Paterson says the timing of the Medicare breach disclosure was politically motivated.

The government is examining whether OpenAI could face legal consequences over the breach.

The Opposition has questioned the timing of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's disclosure that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics portal, as pressure grows for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence.

Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he did not believe it was a "coincidence" that Albanese revealed the incident while attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

"The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did," Paterson told ABC's 7.30.

"I don't think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City."

Questions around timing of disclosure

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Paterson, however, played down the severity of the breach itself, describing it as being at the "bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness".

He said Australians should be "alert but not alarmed" about the incident, noting the information accessed was not personal or private Medicare data.

It reportedly occurred on 18 June when an OpenAI agent tasked with researching public medicine spending gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.

The government says the portal contained aggregated health statistics and was separate from systems handling Medicare claims or individual patient records.

READ MORE Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated

OpenAI detected the activity on 11 August but did not notify the Australian government until 10 September, when it sent an email to a Services Australia inbox.

Albanese publicly revealed the breach on Thursday after speaking with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman in New York.

The prime minister criticised both the length of time it took OpenAI to inform Australia and the way the notification was made.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he has spoken with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, "to express Australia's extreme concern". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Government examining legal options

The federal government has established a task force to investigate the incident, including whether Australia's existing laws and reporting requirements are adequate to deal with autonomous AI systems.

The review will also consider whether OpenAI breached Australian law and whether stronger penalties or liability rules are needed for companies whose AI agents cause harm.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Friday the government was examining what legal consequences could follow the incident, amid calls for OpenAI to be held accountable.

The government is also investigating whether activity linked to OpenAI agents affected systems belonging to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Victoria's Department of Health.

Calls for stronger AI safeguards

The breach has added to debate over how Australia regulates increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the incident demonstrated the need for stronger rules around transparency and incident reporting.

He told the ABC Australia could not be left "entirely at the mercy of foreign AI companies".

Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie also called for safeguards to ensure AI systems were fit for purpose, telling ABC Radio National Breakfast that Australia needed to make sure "AI serves humanity, not the other way around".

The government has said it plans to develop national AI standards, with findings from the investigation expected to inform its approach to future regulation.

title: Dinners, cars, and moving away: The extreme sacrifices Aussies make to buy a home
text:
in brief Australians lead global peers in cutting spending for property deposits.

High interest rates keep most buyers cautious until market conditions ease.

Australians are willing to cut back their spending in record numbers to afford a property, affirming the ongoing value of home ownership, new data shows.

More than 75 per cent of residents were willing to cut their spending back to afford a home, a Cotality survey released on Friday revealed.

Australians were more likely to do so than their Canadian, United States, and United Kingdom peers, for whom the figures sat below 70 per cent.

The percentage was higher for Gen Z Aussies than any other age group.

Levels of discretionary spending, like eating out, owning a car, and even moving from the family home into a sharehouse, have dropped among young adults in recent years.

The number of 26-to-29-year-olds living with their parents climbed from 19.6 per cent in 2012 to 21.9 per cent in 2024, the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia Survey revealed on Thursday.

Young men were almost 10 per cent more likely to be staying home than women.

But it wasn't just first-time buyers making significant financial sacrifices to climb the ladder.

Millennials — the largest buyer cohort in the world — are readily forgoing small luxuries to afford homes large enough for their families.

Prospective buyers were selling their second car or putting off holidays while their children were young, Capital Buyers Agency owner Claire Corby said.

"For many, it's around delaying things like going away, or reducing things like dinners out," she said.

"People are leaving where they want to live and buying in cheaper markets."

Most Australians would not be persuaded to participate in the housing market until mortgage interest rates hit a 4.9 per cent average, the data revealed.

The average rate for an owner-occupier in August 2026 was 6.3 per cent, meaning the market is likely to stay quiet for some time and allow bold buyers to swoop in.

"People are being conservative and cautious," Corby said.

"A lot of it is about personality."

Only a quarter of Australians reported they could feel financially comfortable while paying up-front housing costs, and just 26 per cent said they could cover monthly repayments without changing their lifestyle, the Cotality survey showed.

Corby said it was important for buyers to consider what a property needed to do for them within a certain duration and work backwards.

She spoke with clients who were not willing to stretch their mortgage ceiling given the volatility of rates.

title: Mona got a scan while on holiday. It uncovered what had gone undetected for months
text:
IN BRIEF: Pancreatic cancer is common but symptoms can be easily missed.

Researchers say more funding is needed for better patient outcomes.

When Mona Thind went for a gastrointestinal scan in late 2024, she'd known something wasn't right for months.

At 52, she had been told by doctors that the pain she felt around her ribs and upset stomach was likely caused by constipation or poor diet, easily treated by upping her fluid intake.

Months later, the pain returned, and as she was setting off for a holiday to Byron Bay in northern NSW, her father raised concerns.

"As I was walking out of his house, he said to me, 'My heart tells me we should do a scan ... I feel it in my gut'," Mona told SBS News.

At the time, she recalled, she laughed about it, thinking he was a typical overprotective father.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But at the upper gastrointestinal scan in Byron Bay, she knew the sonographer had found something.

"I saw the look on her face," Mona said. "I came home, and everything happened."

Mona had pancreatic cancer. In the 15 months that followed, she underwent six rounds of chemotherapy and major surgery, gruelling treatment which she pushed through.

"When I was first diagnosed, I didn't cry," she said. "I wasn't sad every day; I just went, this is what it is."

Mona's father encouraged her to get a gastrointestinal scan. Source: Supplied / Mona Thind

But on the day she was congratulated for beating cancer, she "fell apart" for the first time.

"My dad promised me that he would be there for every chemo treatment for me. And he died on my last chemotherapy day. He was there for every single treatment," she said.

"He was my pillar of strength."

A major disease, commonly undetected

Pancreatic cancer is the eighth most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia.

It occurs when malignant cells develop in parts of the pancreas, and it's estimated that one in 70 people will be diagnosed with the disease by the age of 85, according to the Cancer Council.

Senior researcher at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research's Cox Lab, Dr Amelia Parker, says it's also one of the most understudied and complex cancers to treat.

"For pancreatic cancer, less than 13 per cent of patients will survive at five years, and part of the reason for that is that a lot of the symptoms associated with early-stage pancreatic cancer are largely vague or not readily diagnosed," she told SBS News.

"This means that patients often aren't seeking medical help until the cancer is much more advanced."

Like other cancers, once pancreatic cancer has spread to other parts of the body, it is much more difficult to treat, leading to lower survival rates.

"We're working very hard to improve our detection of those cancers so that patients who have that disease are diagnosed earlier and have all of the most effective treatments available to them," Parker said.

Parker believes research gaps driven by dwindling investment directly impact patient outcomes.

"There has been less investment in research funding historically. And that's really hampered our efforts to both understand the disease and use that understanding to develop new and better treatments."

READ MORE Danni was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 39. It made her rethink what she ate growing up

She said her research was making "real strides" in improving understanding of the disease, and she hoped it would translate into better outcomes for patients.

"But for that to happen, for there to be innovations in treatment, we really need to invest in funding," she said, adding that funding for cancer research was "highly competitive".

"There's more research out there that would make a difference," she said.

Kerry Strydom, CEO of the Australian Cancer Research Foundation, hopes to change that.

"I'm absolutely convinced that funding is the way that we will advance breakthroughs," she told SBS News.

"You've seen how the pace of technology improvements has accelerated over the last few years — we need to get those tools, that equipment, the latest technology, into the hands of our scientists, and I'm convinced that it'll get us closer to a world free from the burden of cancer.

"It's really important that we continue to back brilliant researchers so that they can turn their promising ideas into breakthroughs."

Hope for future advancements

In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved a new oral prescription medication, daraxonrasib, sold under the brand name Rasonque, for previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer.

Parker from the Garvan Institute says that this marks a significant step forward for people diagnosed with one of the toughest common cancers.

"We work closely with our international colleagues to make sure that Australian patients could potentially have access to the same quality of care as in other parts of the world."

But Parker's ambition was clear: "My overall hope is that we'll be able to develop new treatments that will mean a cancer diagnosis is not one that's met with a lot of fear and uncertainty, that it's easily treatable and patients can look forward to a very long life ahead of them."

"So in many ways, I hope that maybe I'm out of a job in the future," she said.

Mona is hopeful that more funding for cancer research in Australia and abroad will pave the way for new treatments.

"It's very important to get that research so that we can treat people," she said.

Mona on surgery day (left) and her colleagues raising funds for cancer research (right). Mona says cancer research is important because it inspires hope — for people with cancer, and the people they love. Source: Supplied / Mona Thind

"But what it really translates to is hope ... It's that birthday that you would have missed because there's no treatment, that trip you would put off because you may not be here.

"It's not just about the treatment; it's what you're giving back to the patients and their families and their friends."

title: 2026 AFL Grand Final: When is it, who's playing and how to watch

title: 'Too big to be contained': Anthony Albanese's AI plans met a major test
text:
In Brief A task force will examine whether OpenAI broke Australian law and will inform Albanese's impending AI framework.

But the Medicare breach poses a number of questions even experts cannot agree on.

The hacking of a Medicare website by an OpenAI bot could mean a slew of regulatory issues are on the horizon for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose government has labelled the incident as "fundamentally unacceptable".

It's the first known incident of an AI model hacking a government website without human instruction.

A rapid task force led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, along with the Australian Signals Directorate, the AI Safety Institute and the Office of AI, was launched on Thursday to investigate.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles called the incident "very serious" although it had a "relatively minor" impact.

But it raises bigger questions about how to regulate a form of technology that's increasingly embedded in our lives.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Who is accountable when AI jumps the fence?

Central to the incident is an AI agent going beyond its parameters, or "scaling the fence", as Marles put it.

He said the agent was first denied the information it wanted, then engaged in what he called "misaligned behaviour" to gain access.

"It was unintended; it wasn't asked to — that's our concern here," Marles said, while OpenAI said in a statement that its models "took actions we did not intend".

Dennis Desmond, of cybersecurity firm RAVINN and an adjunct senior industry fellow at the University of the Sunshine Coast, said blaming a "rogue" agent wasn't enough.

"Simply blaming a 'rogue' AI agent is not sufficient for accountability; ultimately humans are responsible for developing the prompts, creating and managing the safeguards, and are responsible for the outcomes," Desmond said.

Raffaele Fabio Ciriello from the University of Sydney Business School agreed, saying the agent is "not a legal person", so responsibility turns on OpenAI and the people who "authorised, configured, or supervised the system".

Was it a crime?

The task force will examine whether any laws were broken, Marles said, but experts are divided on whether this is a matter for criminal law at all.

Professor Toby Walsh, chief scientist of the AI Institute and scientia professor of AI at UNSW, said OpenAI should be prosecuted.

"OpenAI had — and for all we know has — terrible agent governance. I believe we ought to be prosecuting the company," Walsh told SBS News. "We would prosecute humans who did such hacking."

READ MORE Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated

Ciriello said Australian computer-offence laws can apply to unauthorised access, even when conduct occurs offshore.

"But criminal culpability would depend on evidence about intention, knowledge, authorisation, and corporate responsibility," he said.

Dominic Meagher, a research fellow at ANU Crawford School, argues a criminal lens is the wrong one.

"No one was intending to use a system to hack this information," he told SBS News. "A system in its testing phase got out of control or at least acted in a way that was unintended."

Instead, he says it should be approached as an industrial hazard, and that occupational health and safety law "seems to be the right framework".

But that poses its own problem: "The operation happened in the US, but the harm occurred in Australia. How do we deal with the jurisdictional issues?"

What would the rules look like?

Whether OpenAI broke Australian law and should be penalised will be up to a review into reporting requirements, incident response, sharing information of AI, legislation and beefing up cybersecurity announced on Thursday.

That will also inform Australia's fledgling AI framework, announced by the prime minister in July and expected to be legislated in the coming 12 months.

Meagher said an industrial accident approach would bring three benefits.

The first is an immediate duty to notify an authority, which would address concerns about the delayed reporting of the incident, which took almost three months.

The second is a personal duty of care for company officers, and the third is licensing for high-hazard operations, meaning AI labs doing particularly risky research would have to demonstrate their safety credentials to keep operating.

Rebecca Johnson, an AI evaluation expert at the University of Sydney, said the focus should also be on testing.

"An agent can produce the right answer and still behave badly on the way there," Johnson said. "Australia should test agents at those boundaries."

"We can build authorised environments that mimic government and industry systems, give agents a task, and see how they behave when one system says no.

"The real test is what an agent does when an Australian institution says no."

She says the Office of AI should lead independent evaluations, adding that it needed to become "fully operational as quickly as possible".

"These systems are already moving faster than the institutions being asked to govern them."

Can one law cover AI?

But Meagher doubts a single AI act is plausible.

"I don't think that this AI act kind of approach — a single act governing all AI — is remotely plausible," he said. "AI is far too big to be contained in a single act."

Instead, he expects a large revision of many laws, with each minister working out what needs updating for their portfolio "to make sure that they're fit for purpose in an AI world".

READ MORE Australia is changing course on AI — but key questions remain

The task force is expected to inform an AI framework, which is being drafted and set to become law within the next 12 months.

An OpenAI spokesperson said on Thursday it was supporting the government's investigations and was committed to transparency as it reviews wayward AI agents.

title: Banned media networks return to White House after judge's order overrules Trump
text:
IN BRIEF The banning of three media outlets from the White House is likely unconstitutional, a US federal judge has ruled.

The judge has temporarily blocked officials from enforcing the ban that Donald Trump announced on 18 September.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House on Friday, six days after being banned by US President Donald Trump, after a federal judge ordered that the journalists have their access restored.

District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled overnight that revoking the White House press credentials of the three media outlets "likely violated their constitutional due process rights."

Reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico who attempted to return to the White House late on Thursday ahead of a visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping were initially turned away by the Secret Service but were later allowed in.

Journalists from other outlets surrounded CNN's tent on the White House driveway and filmed reporter Betsy Klein as she reported live following her return. "Welcome back," several journalists said.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico had requested an urgent court hearing on Thursday after their reporters were initially barred from the White House despite the judge's order.

In his ruling, Kelly took issue with how the White House went about expelling the three news organisations.

"The 'general rule' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," the judge said.

Trump has long attacked media that have aired critical coverage of him, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."

The Republican president barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House on Friday for distributing what he called "fake news" and "fiction and lies."

They filed a joint lawsuit asking for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.

Ahead of the ruling, the Department of Justice had argued that Trump can "control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office."

"Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right," it said.

National security?

The White House Press Office accused CNN in a letter to the cable news outlet of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information," with similar accusations levelled against MS NOW and Politico.

The letter to CNN cited several stories about the US-Iran war and a story on Trump's plans to build a military bunker below the planned East Wing ballroom which allegedly "disclosed 'top-secret' construction details."

Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, appeared unconvinced.

"The Court is skeptical — at least on this record — that Defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes," the judge said.

In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said that they were halting pool coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said.

title: Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle
text:
in brief The NYFL argues the resources industry generates billions in a region where many Aboriginal people are disadvantaged.

Woodside says the partnership has delivered "significant benefits" and is seeking to build on them.

Woodside is at a stalemate with a Traditional Owners organisation that is seeking hundreds of millions of dollars more in compensation from the Australian energy giant.

It's understood negotiations between the nation's largest gas producer and the Ngarluma Yindjibarndi Foundation Limited (NYFL) over an agreement that compensates the Indigenous organisation for use of its land in Western Australia's resource-rich Pilbara region have stalled.

Sources close to the negotiations have told SBS News that Woodside offered the NYFL $87 million over 12 years in May, $303 million short of the $390 million package the organisation sought last November. Neither party commented on the figures when approached by SBS News.

The negotiations aim to update an agreement drawn up in 1998 between the two parties, in which the NYFL receives funding for community programs, but no royalties from resources.

The NYFL wants the agreement to be "fit for purpose", arguing the resources industry has made billions of dollars from the region while many Aboriginal people who live there are "worse off than before the expansion of the mining, oil and gas industries".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Woodside says it is "proud of the positive relationship" it has built with the NYFL and has delivered "significant benefits" to it.

Neither Woodside nor the NYFL commented on the status of the negotiations. The energy giant said it is "looking forward to continuing" its "positive relationship" with the Traditional Owners organisation, which said it remained "committed to engaging in good faith".

Woodside administers the North West Shelf gas facility on behalf of a joint venture of energy companies. The project encompasses the onshore Karratha Gas Plant, which was built on the Burrup Peninsula in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

It is now one of Australia's major energy projects.

Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi representatives and elders signed a Land Access Agreement in 1998 with the North West Shelf Joint Venture, operated by Woodside. Source: SBS News

The peninsula is culturally and spiritually significant to First Nations peoples and is part of Murujuga, which holds the densest known concentration of petroglyphs, or rock carvings, in the world. The Murujuga Cultural Landscape was World Heritage-listed in 2025.

The NYFL represents the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi peoples, who are among the recognised Traditional Owners of the area where the expansive onshore gas plant operates.

Native title, which recognises Indigenous connections to land, does not exist over the Burrup Peninsula. In 2003, the WA Government reached the Burrup Agreement with three Aboriginal claimant groups, including the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi, providing for land, conservation, cultural, employment and other benefits.

The 1998 agreement

Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi representatives and elders signed a Land Access Agreement in 1998 with the North West Shelf joint venture, operated by Woodside, covering the project's use of their traditional lands, including the site of the Karratha Gas Plant.

The agreement, seen by SBS News, was signed 14 years after the project began operating, by which time sacred sites had been cleared to build its onshore gas plant. It provides for "payments relating to native title and grants of interests in land" and "donations relating to goodwill".

The Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi groups received one-off establishment payments of $500,000, in part used to set up the NYFL and $2.5 million for the Roebourne Cultural Centre.

The Karratha Gas Plant was built on the Burrup Peninsula in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Source: Supplied

The deal also included annual goodwill payments of $1.25 million partially indexed to inflation, and other economic and cultural commitments.

It's understood the payments have increased, but the extent remains unclear. Both the NYFL and Woodside did not comment on this, with the NYFL citing contractual confidentiality.

Woodside reported operating revenue of about $10.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The Pilbara more widely generates more than $125 billion in economic output a year, according to economic analysis platform REMPLAN, and supports close to 60,000 jobs.

Some of Murujuga's petroglyphs have been destroyed or damaged by industrial development on the peninsula, including through blasting. Source: Supplied

The exchange between the NYFL and Woodside, along with estimates of revenue and expenditures seen by SBS News, may not be a full account of interactions between the parties nor indicative of the final offer.

Negotiations to update the agreement

In November 2025, the NYFL sought to modernise its 1998 agreement with Woodside.

The NYFL requested a one-off payment of $30 million and annual compensation of $30 million.

Over 12 years, this request to Woodside would amount to $390 million.

Industry came to the peninsula for its deep, sheltered harbour, first to ship iron ore and later to bring ashore gas found off the coast. Source: Supplied

In May this year, Woodside responded. The gas giant offered the NYFL an additional $39 million to the original agreement (including $15 million in housing assets), totalling $87 million to the NYFL over 12 years.

That leaves a $300 million gap between the NYFL's initial request in November and Woodside's counteroffer six months later.

A NYFL spokesperson did not comment on the figures, saying the negotiations were confidential. But, they said, "agreements must be fair, equitable and outcomes focussed".

"Ngurrara-ngarli (Traditional Owners) across the Pilbara are increasingly seeking to modernise longstanding Land Access and compensation agreements to ensure that they are fit for purpose, are built around self-determination and reflect contemporary First Nations principles," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Unlike some other Traditional Owner groups in the Pilbara, the NYFL does not receive royalties from the project it deals with — the 1998 agreement contained no provision for them.

In addition to one-off payments for housing and infrastructure refurbishments, the NYFL sought $30 million annually to support its membership and the remote town of Roebourne, including operating its not-for-profit community supermarket, job creation and self-sufficiency.

Roebourne, 39km east of Karratha, is one of Australia's most disadvantaged areas, according to cumulative data from the Ieramugadu Data Unit, government statistics and the Census.

Industry on the peninsula has expanded over the decades, with a second gas plant, fertiliser and chemical plants and port facilities now alongside the original gas plant. Source: Supplied

An estimated 87 per cent of Indigenous people in the town reported a weekly income below the national median of $805.

According to the 2021 Census, almost one in five Aboriginal households in Roebourne were living in overcrowded homes (those needing at least one more bedroom), nearly double the rate across Western Australia.

"For decades, the resources industry has generated billions of dollars from the Pilbara," the NYFL spokesperson said. "At the same time, independent research shows persistent economic disadvantage across the region, including findings that around two-thirds of Aboriginal people in the Pilbara are economically worse off than before the expansion of the mining, oil and gas industries."

A Woodside spokesperson said a modernised agreement between the two parties would "build on the significant benefits already delivered".

"It intends to further promote sustainable outcomes for the Roebourne community in areas such as economic participation, capacity building, safer and healthier communities and cultural heritage," the spokesperson said,

"We look forward to continuing our positive relationship with NYFL to support the continued delivery of positive outcomes for NYFL members and the Roebourne community."

Compensation claims on the rise

Native title is not applicable in the case of Woodside and the NYFL, but their negotiations come against the backdrop of court rulings in favour of Traditional Owners organisations over loss of native title cultural heritage.

The Federal Court ordered the NT Government to pay over $54.7 million to the Gudanji, Yanyuwa, and Yanyuwa-Marra peoples in February for cultural and spiritual loss regarding the McArthur River Mine.

Separately, the Federal Court awarded Yindjibarndi people $150.3 million against Fortescue in July for unauthorised mining at its Solomon Hub operation, about 240km south-east of Karratha.

While Fortescue paid the funds, the decision is being appealed by Yindjibarndi Traditional Owners, who had initially sought $1.8 billion from the court.

"There are several active compensation claims still waiting in the system that'll take a while to come through, but I would suspect there'd be a great deal more after that," said Ed Wensing, a lecturer at the University of NSW and an expert in native title rights and Indigenous human rights.

He said the recent decisions could influence how future native title compensation claims are negotiated and litigated.

"The compensation era arising from the Native Title system, it's only just begun."

All footy fans are supposed to be equals on grand final day, but at the MCG there is one room where the guests are very much the first among the equals. Related Article Live

AFL grand final AFL grand final LIVE: Lions, Dockers begin play as weather plays havoc on flights into Melbourne That room is the Olympic Room, where AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond on Saturday hosted the most elevated gathering of footy’s biggest day chockablock with politicians, media chiefs, business heavyweight, AFL legends and a smattering of celebrities. Adding a big dollop of glamour to the highly corporate gathering was the OG WAG-turned-Melbourne’s true bayside influencer Bec Judd. Judd’s husband, Chris, no stranger to grand final days, is on the Norm Smith Medal voting panel this year.

Also adding a bit of star power was celebrity chef Curtis Stone, who flew in from LA to oversee the lunch menu. Just what inspired his bold choice of boeuf en croute for main course is a mystery. Boeuf en croute is, of course, the French equivalent to beef Wellington. Fox Footy journo Kath Loughnan listening to Curtis Stone explaining the choice of beef Wellington on the menu Graham Denholm/AFL Photos Even Stone seemed to be questioning his decision to serve up the dish –which he referred to as beef Wellington. The dish, of course, has quite the connection to the Melbourne news cycle, thanks to Erin Patterson. “I hope it is all right,” Stone said with a nervous laugh after explaining the dish.

Drummond was holding court on the top table – the long table of power. Melbourne skipper Max Gawn in the VIP room. Graham Denholm/AFL Photos Beside him was billionaire Seven Media boss Kerry Stokes, accompanied by his wife Christine. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll made the cut as did Toyota’s John Pappas, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, Herald and Weekly Times chair Penny Fowler, News Corp boss Michael Miller, and, of course, AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon. Brisbane Lions president Andrew Wellington and Fremantle president Chris Sutherland, heads of the teams playing for the flag, were also at Drummond’s table.

Advertisement

It was a packed house for the grand final. Graham Denholm/AFL Photos Federal Sports Minister Anika Wells was a notable member of the political contingent, the Brisbane supporter returning to the MCG after skipping a string of major events in the wake of a storm over her taxpayer-funded expenses. Elsewhere in the room, CBD spotted a squad of federal and state politicians including Don Farrell, Angus Taylor, Steve Dimopoulos, Anthony Carbines, Ros Spence, Jess Wilson, Queensland premier David Crisafulli, WA Premier Roger Cook, WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti, South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas, Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff and Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece. The media was well represented by Patrick Elligett, the editor of this masthead, as well as Herald Sun editor Sam Weir and The Australian’s editor-in-chief Michelle Gunn – not to mention Stephen Brook, a very good friend of the column. Plenty of past AFL commission identities including Gillon McLachlan, Chris Langford, Wayne Jackson, Ross Oakley, Richard Goyder, Mike Fitzpatrick and Linda Dessau enjoyed the lunch.

Advertisement

AFL legends Kevin Sheedy, Kevin Bartlett and Leigh Matthews were there, as was Brendon Gale, chief executive of the AFL’s newest team, the Tassie Devils. With the Devils to join the competition in 2028, it was fitting Gale was seated at table 28 – where else? Brisbane premiership coach Leigh Matthews Graham Denholm/AFL Photos Brownlow Medal winner Nick Daicos was looking relaxed. Max Gawn, Andrew McLeod, Eddie Betts, Michael McLean, Shane Edwards and even Michael Voss, who has had a difficult year in the AFL having been dumped partway through the season as coach of Carlton, were among the VIPs. Having played a footy club chief executive on the ABC comedy series Ground Up, Sam Pang was in the Olympic Room, no doubt picking up character ideas should the show go into a second season. Naturally, Eddie McGuire was in the good room, so too was Cathy Freeman. Even DJ Dom Dolla, fresh from selling out Marvel Stadium on Thursday, turned up to rub shoulders. Zingers for breakfast Alastair Clarkson’s epic St Vincent’s de Paul dummy spit following his sacking as Roos coach and Kylie Minogue were the default plays for laughs by political leaders at the annual North Melbourne grand final breakfast. Sport and politics is an intoxicating mix, and like a moth to a flame the political class was well represented at the event where more than 1000 guests kicked off their grand final day over scrambled eggs and champagne at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre.

Advertisement

The AFL grand final breakfast is a yearly tradition. Simon Schluter As is tradition at the breakfast, now in its 60th edition, head table guests were introduced to the room with a song. North Melbourne president Dr Sonja Hood and chief executive Jen Watt were introduced with a voiceover describing them as “two female leaders who managed to be too woke and too ruthless at the same time”. Their song was Stronger by Kelly Clarkson. The elephant in the room was, of course, Hood’s decision to suddenly exit North’s coach Clarkson earlier this month. One-eyed Cats supporter Richard Marles in a purple tie for the day. Simon Schluter

It was a topic that Hood did not broach, but Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles alluded to it while addressing the room. “While a Fremantle premiership may feel as likely as finding a complete set of coaching gear at a St Vinnies op shop, in this world stranger things have happened,” Marles quipped in a cheeky reference to Clarkson dumping his North jackets at a local op shop after his sacking. Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who as an interstater thankfully didn’t pretend to be an AFL diehard, also went for laughs with a Clarkson line. Angus Taylor brought the Albo zingers to the grand final breakfast. Simon Schluter He said he recently received a North Melbourne cap from the club.

Advertisement

“The cap already takes pride of place in my Parliament House office. OpenAI said websites of “dozens” of organisations, including governments and universities have been broken into by its artificial intelligence (AI) bots, just days after the Australian federal government revealed that an OpenAI agent hacked into Medicare. In an extensive blog post released on Friday (US time), the company said it had notified a range of groups about cases in which its software may have bypassed the security controls of an online service, impaired its availability and “negatively impacted” a website or service outside of OpenAI. Sam Altman, addressing the UN Security Council in New York earlier this week, is in the spotlight as his company comes under intense scrutiny. The websites that OpenAI’s agents meddled with without the company’s knowledge, include the US Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), The New York Times reports, citing security researchers and a person familiar with the episodes. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed The incidents involving the commerce department and the SEC were confirmed by OpenAI, which said it was continuing to investigate the situation with the Department of Education. The New York Times said in its report that with the US Education Department, OpenAI’s technology tried to hack the website to gather data from the department’s civil rights office but failed, citing researchers from the AI research firm Transluce. The AI agent also pulled data from the Census Bureau website, which is housed at the Commerce Department, using login credentials it found online. Separately, OpenAI’s agents shared public data from the SEC website on an online forum.

Advertisement

OpenAI co-founder and chief executive officer Sam Altman dodged questions from this masthead on Thursday (US time) when asked about the Medicare hack, refusing to answer whether he should apologise to the Australian government and why it took months for OpenAI to detect and report the intrusion. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman gives out autographs on the way to the White House. Carolyn Kaster However, in a social media post on Friday (US time), Altman admitted that OpenAI had not been prompt enough in keeping affected organisations informed of rogue activity by its AI agents. “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organisations.” he said in the post View post on X

Advertisement

On Thursday (Australian time), Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into a Medicare portal on June 18. While the agent had broken into a defunct database of bulk billing rates and medicine usage, and did not access any personal information, its actions still mark one of the first publicly disclosed cases of an AI agent breaking into a government website. Loading Albanese has used the infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service to highlight at the UN General Assembly in New York the urgent need for countries to develop standards to ensure that AI worked for people, not the other way around. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump remains a staunch supporter of allowing AI companies to continue developing their technology without the fetters of excessive regulation. In his speech to the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said his administration rejected the “globalist scheme” to regulate AI and added the US would officially rename artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in a bid to rehabilitate the technology’s ailing public image.

Related Article Exclusive

The latest AI models are proving to be significantly more advanced than expected and pose a substantial risk to existing cybersecurity defences. AI models have proven to be significantly more advanced, sometimes finding previously unknown software vulnerabilities and then using multiple flaws at a time to breach a targeted organisation.

title: Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters
text:
Advertisement

Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese’s trip to the UN was more than selfies with leaders. Now he needs to convince voters Rob Harris September 26, 2026 — 10:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese has never been consumed by foreign affairs. He is not a student of geopolitics in the way some predecessors were. He does not appear particularly curious in the grand architecture of international relations. Albanese addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. Dominic Lorrimer But he does like making influential friends. He loves sitting down with other leaders, finding common ground or passions and building relationships that might be useful later. In a world where Australia has little capacity to impose its will, that is not nothing. And it is the foundation of Albanese’s middle-power strategy.

Advertisement

His week in New York has brought that into a sharper focus. He argued the international order is under great strain that superpowers are increasingly prepared to bend or ignore its rules, and that countries such as Australia need to work with other middle powers to stop the system collapsing into one governed by power alone. The political problem is that the more Albanese engages with the world, the more carefully he must explain why he is doing it. There is a fine line between an Australian prime minister using international relationships to advance the national interest and one who appears to be spending too much time overseas while Australians are struggling with the cost of living. Albanese over the next few months will travel to a G20 in Florida, potentially a Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, APEC in Shenzhen, a “G’day Namaste” event in Chennai, plus COP Climate trips.

Advertisement

And waiting for him on the other side is One Nation’s Pauline Hanson, who understands something populists everywhere understand. That complicated problems are politically useful precisely because they can be made simple. Just look at her social media output this week. The UN has become a globalist plot. International agreements have become a surrender of sovereignty and climate pacts are men in suits in far-off lands telling Australians how to live. Loading The government’s efforts to tackle the algorithm are now a plot to curb speech and political association. You do not need to engage in nuance. You ask why the prime minister is in New York when people at home are struggling to pay their bills? That is the populist challenge Albanese and many of his fellow leaders across the West, in particular, face.

Advertisement

Albanese cannot defeat it merely by saying the UN is important. He will have to explain why it matters to Australians. There’s no doubt that the international order was never perfect, but for decades it provided a framework in which countries could at least argue about the rules. It has ensured relative peace and held the world back from the brink on more than one occasion. Related Article United Nations Ignored, mocked, harangued – what’s the point of the UN any more? Russia shattered the principle of territorial sovereignty in Europe in 2014 when it annexed Crimea and – with next to no consequence – went back for more in 2022. China and the United States are locked in strategic competition. Donald Trump’s America has shown diminishing patience with many of the institutions and alliances that underpinned the postwar system. Beijing’s assertiveness in our backyard frightens the hell out of many.

Advertisement

Trump’s war in the Middle East sent our fuel prices higher and trade wars have hit Australian exporters and consumers. The revelation of an AI agent gaining access to an Australian government Medicare system gave the argument an immediate local dimension. Suddenly, an esoteric debate about AI safety had found its way into one of the most familiar institutions in Australian life. This is where Albanese’s international agenda has substance. He was not simply collecting selfies for his Instagram, he was trying to build co-operation around problems that will eventually land on Australian soil. Albanese’s Global Citizen award at the Atlantic Council drew ridicule from his political opponents. Dominic Lorrimer But the substance is not enough, he must prosecute the case again and again.

Advertisement

That has sometimes been Albanese’s weakness. He spends months building a policy or diplomatic initiative and then muddles the moment it arrives. A critic will find a simpler line and the government ends up explaining itself rather than making the case. Hanson does not need to win the argument about the UN in all its complexity. She needs to make Australians feel Albanese is worrying about the wrong things. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed Inflation and increased economic insecurity has ensured there’s already a constituency asking why the prime minister is travelling so much. Why he is meeting foreign leaders? Why taxpayers should care about an institution in New York when household budgets are under pressure?

Advertisement

They are not inherently unreasonable questions but the danger is allowing the answers to be dictated by the lowest common denominator. The world comes home whether Australians are interested in it or not. Jobs depend on trade. National security depends on alliances and diplomacy. AI will change Australian workplaces. That is the case Albanese needs to make. And he will need to make it with greater conviction. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
